tool.name: C++
tool.tagline: Fast, zero-overhead systems language for performance-critical software
tool.description: C++ is a compiled, statically typed language that combines low-level control over memory and hardware with high-level abstractions such as classes, templates and the standard library. It powers game engines, browsers, databases, trading systems, embedded devices and machine-learning runtimes. Learning modern C++ (C++20, with C++23 notes) teaches you how software really runs and lets you write code that is both expressive and as fast as the machine allows.

concepts.name: Compiling and running
concepts.summary: Turn .cpp source files into an executable with a compiler and linker, and switch on the warnings and checks that catch bugs early.
concepts.why: Every C++ program goes through this pipeline, and most confusing build errors make sense once you know its stages.
concepts.body:
C++ is compiled ahead of time. You write source files (`.cpp`), a **compiler** turns each one into machine code in an object file (`.o` / `.obj`), and a **linker** joins the object files and libraries into an executable. The three mainstream compilers are GCC (`g++`), Clang (`clang++`) and MSVC (`cl`).

Each `.cpp` file is compiled on its own as a **translation unit**. First the preprocessor handles lines starting with `#`: `#include <iostream>` literally pastes the contents of that header into your file. Then the compiler checks and translates the code. Only at link time are calls into other files and libraries matched up with their definitions; an "undefined reference" error comes from the linker, not the compiler.

Always say which language standard you want with `-std=c++20` (or `-std=c++23`; on MSVC `/std:c++20`), because compilers default to older or extended dialects. Then turn on help from the compiler:

- `-Wall -Wextra` enable the warnings that flag most real mistakes; treat warnings as bugs (`-Werror` in CI).
- `-g` adds debug info for `gdb`/`lldb`; `-O2` optimises for release builds.
- `-fsanitize=address,undefined` instruments the program to report out-of-bounds access, use-after-free and many kinds of undefined behaviour at run time. Use it in development and tests.

Compiling only what changed is the job of a build system (CMake, covered later); for a single file, one command is enough. Online, Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org) shows what any compiler does with a snippet.
concepts.code:
# hello.cpp contains a main() function
g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -g hello.cpp -o hello
./hello

# development build with run-time bug detectors
clang++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined hello.cpp -o hello

# optimised release build
g++ -std=c++20 -O2 hello.cpp -o hello

# several files: compile each to an object file, then link them
g++ -std=c++20 -c main.cpp -o main.o
g++ -std=c++20 -c util.cpp -o util.o
g++ main.o util.o -o app

# MSVC, from a Developer Command Prompt
cl /std:c++20 /EHsc /W4 hello.cpp
takeaways: Source file -> preprocessor -> compiler -> object file -> linker -> executable
Always pass the standard explicitly: `-std=c++20`
Develop with `-Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined`
pitfalls: Ignoring warnings: many real bugs (uninitialised variables, sign mismatches) show up as warnings first.

quiz.q: You change only util.cpp in a project of main.cpp and util.cpp. What is the minimum work to rebuild?
options: Recompile util.cpp, then link the object files again
Only relink; the linker recompiles changed files
Recompile util.cpp; no link step is needed
quiz.explain: Each .cpp is compiled independently, so only util.o is stale, but the executable must be relinked to include it.

quiz.q: The build fails with "undefined reference to `parse(int)'". Which stage reported it?
quiz.explain: The compiler accepted the declaration; the linker could not find any object file that defines parse(int).

concepts.name: main, input and output
concepts.summary: Write a complete program: the main function, printing with std::cout and reading input with std::cin.
concepts.why: Every program starts in main, and console I/O is how you try out everything else in this course.
concepts.body:
A C++ program starts in `main`. It returns an `int` to the operating system: `0` means success, anything else signals failure. `main` is the one function where you may leave out the `return`; reaching the closing brace returns `0`.

Standard library names live in the namespace `std`, so you write `std::cout`, `std::string` and so on. You get them by including headers: `<iostream>` for console streams, `<string>` for strings.

- `std::cout << x` writes to standard output. `<<` returns the stream, so calls chain: `std::cout << "a" << 1 << '\n';`.
- `std::cerr` is standard error, for diagnostics.
- `std::cin >> x` reads one whitespace-separated value and converts it to the type of `x`. The expression is false if reading failed, so test it.
- `std::getline(std::cin, s)` reads a whole line, spaces included.

Prefer `'\n'` over `std::endl`: `endl` also flushes the buffer, which is slow in loops. A classic gotcha is mixing `>>` and `getline`: after `std::cin >> n` the newline is still waiting in the input, so the next `getline` returns an empty line.

C++20 added `std::format` (header `<format>`) for Python-style formatting, `std::format("{} is {}", name, age)`, and C++23 adds `std::println` in `<print>`, which formats and prints in one call. Streams are still everywhere in existing code, so learn both.

Avoid `using namespace std;` at file scope in real projects; it pulls hundreds of names into scope and causes clashes. Writing `std::` is the norm.
takeaways: `main` returns `int`; 0 means success
`<<` writes, `>>` reads one token, `std::getline` reads a line
Use `'\n'` instead of `std::endl` unless you really need a flush
C++20 `std::format` and C++23 `std::println` are the modern formatting tools
pitfalls: Calling `std::getline` right after `std::cin >> n` and getting an empty string because the newline was left in the input.

quiz.q: The user types `42 apples` and the program runs `std::cin >> n >> word;` with int n and std::string word. What ends up in word?
quiz.explain: >> skips leading whitespace and reads one token, so n gets 42 and word gets apples.

quiz.q: Why is `'\n'` usually preferred over `std::endl`?
options: endl does not work on Windows
endl also flushes the stream, which is slow when done often
quiz.explain: Both end the line, but std::endl forces a flush every time, which costs a system call.

concepts.name: Variables and fundamental types
concepts.summary: Declare variables of the built-in types (int, double, bool, char and friends) and know their sizes, limits and arithmetic rules.
concepts.why: C++ makes you choose types explicitly, and the rules for sizes, overflow and conversions cause real bugs if you don't know them.
concepts.body:
A variable has a type fixed at compile time: `int count = 0;`. The fundamental types are:

- Integers: `short`, `int`, `long`, `long long`, each with an `unsigned` variant. The standard only guarantees minimum widths (`int` at least 16 bits, `long long` at least 64); on every mainstream platform `int` is 32 bits.
- `std::size_t`: unsigned, the type of sizes and indexes (`sizeof`, `.size()`).
- Exact widths from `<cstdint>`: `std::int32_t`, `std::uint64_t`, ... for file formats and protocols.
- Floating point: `float` (32-bit), `double` (64-bit, the default for literals like `1.5`).
- `bool` (`true`/`false`) and `char` (one byte, holds a character such as `'A'`).

`sizeof(T)` gives a size in bytes and `std::numeric_limits<T>` (header `<limits>`) gives ranges. Literals can use digit separators (`1'000'000`) and suffixes (`2.5f` is a float, `10u` unsigned, `10LL` long long).

Know the arithmetic rules. Integer division truncates: `7 / 2` is `3`; make one operand a double (`7 / 2.0`) for `3.5`. Unsigned arithmetic wraps around modulo 2^N, so `0u - 1` is a huge number. Signed overflow is **undefined behaviour**: the compiler assumes it never happens, and the result is not guaranteed to wrap.

A local variable without an initializer, like `int x;`, holds garbage, and reading it is undefined behaviour. Initialize every variable when you declare it. Use `const` for values that never change: `const double tax_rate = 0.2;`.
takeaways: Sizes are platform-dependent; use `<cstdint>` types when the exact width matters
Integer division truncates; unsigned wraps; signed overflow is undefined behaviour
Always initialise variables when you declare them
pitfalls: Reading an uninitialised local (`int x; x++;`) — it is undefined behaviour, not zero.

quiz.q: What does `int r = 9 / 4 * 2.0;` store in r?
quiz.explain: 9 / 4 is integer division giving 2, times 2.0 is 4.0, converted to int 4.

quiz.q: Which statement about `int` overflow, as in INT_MAX + 1, is correct?
options: It wraps to INT_MIN on all platforms
quiz.explain: Signed integer overflow is undefined behaviour; only unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap.

concepts.name: auto and brace initialization
concepts.summary: Let the compiler deduce types with auto, and use brace initialization to get safe, uniform initialization without narrowing.
concepts.why: Modern C++ code uses auto and {} everywhere; knowing their exact rules avoids silent copies and surprising vector sizes.
concepts.body:
`auto` asks the compiler to deduce a variable's type from its initializer: `auto n = 42;` is an `int`, `auto d = 2.5;` a `double`. It shines with long type names (iterators, lambdas) and keeps code correct when types change.

The rule to remember: plain `auto` makes a **copy** and drops top-level `const` and references. If `ref` is a `const std::vector<int>&`, then `auto v = ref;` copies the whole vector. Write `const auto& v = ref;` to bind without copying, or `auto&` when you want to modify the original.

C++ has several initialization syntaxes. **Brace initialization** works for everything and is the safest:

- `int x{5};` or `int x = {5};`
- `int zero{};` value-initializes to `0` (also `nullptr`, `false`, empty objects).
- Braces reject **narrowing**: `int n{3.7};` is a compile error, while `int n = 3.7;` silently truncates to `3`.
- `Widget w{};` always creates an object, while `Widget w();` declares a function (the "most vexing parse").

The one big gotcha: if a class has a constructor taking `std::initializer_list`, braces prefer it. `std::vector<int> a(3, 7);` is three sevens, but `std::vector<int> b{3, 7};` is the two elements 3 and 7. Use parentheses when you mean "count and value".

Another subtle one: `auto s = "hi";` deduces `const char*`, not `std::string`. Write `std::string s = "hi";` or use the `s` literal suffix.

Use `auto` where the type is obvious or noisy, and spell the type where it documents intent.
takeaways: `auto` copies and drops `const`/`&`; use `const auto&` to avoid copies
Braces forbid narrowing and `{}` zero-initialises
Braces prefer `initializer_list` constructors: `vector{3, 7}` has two elements
pitfalls: Writing `std::vector<int> v{n};` expecting n elements — it creates one element with value n.

quiz.q: What is the type of `x` in `const std::string& r = name; auto x = r;`?
quiz.explain: Plain auto drops references and top-level const, so x is a new std::string copy.

quiz.q: How many elements does `std::vector<int> v{5, 0};` contain?
quiz.explain: Braces select the initializer_list constructor, so v holds the two values 5 and 0.

concepts.name: Operators and expressions
concepts.summary: Arithmetic, comparison, logical and bitwise operators, plus the precedence and conversion rules that trip people up.
concepts.why: Expressions are the bulk of any program, and a few C++ operator rules (precedence, signed/unsigned mixing) cause classic bugs.
concepts.body:
The arithmetic operators are `+ - * / %`, with compound forms like `+=` and `*=`. `%` is the remainder; with negative operands division truncates toward zero, so `-7 / 2` is `-3` and `-7 % 2` is `-1`.

`++i` increments and yields the new value; `i++` yields the old value. On their own as statements they're equivalent; prefer `++i` as a habit (for iterators it can be cheaper).

Comparisons (`== != < <= > >=`) yield `bool`. The logical operators `&&`, `||` and `!` **short-circuit**: in `count != 0 && total / count > 10` the division is never evaluated when `count` is 0. That is guaranteed and widely relied upon.

The bitwise operators `& | ^ ~ << >>` work on the bits of integers; use unsigned types for bit manipulation. Watch precedence: `==` binds tighter than `&`, so `flags & mask == 0` means `flags & (mask == 0)`. When in doubt, add parentheses.

The conditional operator `cond ? a : b` picks one of two values and is handy for initializing `const` variables.

Mixed-type expressions are converted to a common type. The nasty case is signed with unsigned: the signed value is converted to unsigned, so `-1 < 0u` is **false** because -1 becomes 4294967295. Compilers warn about this (`-Wall` enables `-Wsign-compare`); C++20 adds `std::cmp_less` and friends in `<utility>` that compare mixed integers correctly. This bites most often when comparing an `int` index with `v.size()`.

Finally, `=` assigns and `==` compares. `if (x = 5)` compiles (with a warning) and is always true.
takeaways: `&&` and `||` short-circuit, which makes guards like `p && p->ok` safe
Comparing signed with unsigned converts the signed side: `-1 < 0u` is false
`==` binds tighter than `&`, `|`, `^`: parenthesise bit tests
pitfalls: Comparing `int i` with `v.size()` when i can be negative — use `std::ssize(v)` or `std::cmp_less`.

quiz.q: What does `std::cout << (5 & 4 == 4);` print?
quiz.explain: 4 == 4 is evaluated first giving true (1), and 5 & 1 is 1.

quiz.q: After `int i = 3; int j = i++ * 2;`, what are i and j?
quiz.explain: i++ yields the old value 3, so j is 6, and i becomes 4.

concepts.name: Branches and loops
concepts.summary: Control flow with if, switch, while, do-while, classic for and range-based for, including if-with-initializer.
concepts.why: Branching and looping are the core of every algorithm, and C++ has a few forms (range-for, init-statements) that make them safer.
concepts.body:
`if (cond) { ... } else if (other) { ... } else { ... }` works as in most languages. Always use braces in real code; a dangling `else` or an added second line under an unbraced `if` is a classic bug.

Since C++17, `if` and `switch` can declare a variable scoped to the statement: `if (auto it = m.find(k); it != m.end()) { ... }`. The variable doesn't leak into the surrounding code.

`switch` jumps to a matching `case` label on an integer, `char` or enum value. Execution falls through into the next case unless you `break`; several labels can share code deliberately, and `[[fallthrough]];` marks intentional fall-through so the compiler doesn't warn. `default` handles everything else. You can't switch on strings.

Loops:

- `while (cond) { ... }` checks before each iteration; `do { ... } while (cond);` runs the body at least once.
- `for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)` is the counting loop.
- **Range-based for**, `for (int x : v)`, visits every element of a container or array. Use `for (const auto& x : v)` to avoid copying big elements and `for (auto& x : v)` to modify them.

`break` leaves the innermost loop or switch and `continue` jumps to the next iteration. There's no labelled break; to exit nested loops, move them into a function and `return`.

Prefer range-for whenever you don't need the index; it can't go out of bounds. When you do need an index into a container, use `std::size_t` (or C++20 `std::ssize` for a signed size) to avoid signed/unsigned warnings.
takeaways: Use `for (const auto& x : c)` to visit elements without copying
`switch` falls through without `break`; mark intentional cases with `[[fallthrough]]`
`if (init; cond)` keeps helper variables scoped to the branch
pitfalls: Forgetting `break` in a switch case, so the next case's code runs too.

quiz.q: With `int x = 2;`, what does this print? `switch (x) { case 1: std::cout << 'a'; case 2: std::cout << 'b'; case 3: std::cout << 'c'; break; default: std::cout << 'd'; }`
quiz.explain: Execution starts at case 2 and falls through into case 3 until the break.

quiz.q: Which loop is the right choice to double every element of `std::vector<int> v` in place?
quiz.explain: Only a non-const reference refers to the elements themselves; the others copy or forbid modification.

concepts.name: Functions
concepts.summary: Declare and define functions, pass arguments by value, return results, and understand declarations versus definitions.
concepts.why: Functions are the unit of reuse and testing, and C++'s declare-before-use and pass-by-value rules shape how code is organised.
concepts.body:
A function has a return type, a name, parameters and a body: `int square(int x) { return x * x; }`. Use `void` when it returns nothing. A non-void function must return a value on every path; falling off the end is undefined behaviour (compilers warn with `-Wall`).

C++ compiles top to bottom, so a function must be **declared** before it is called. A declaration (a prototype) is the signature followed by a semicolon: `int square(int x);`. The **definition** with the body can come later or live in another file. This split is exactly how headers work: headers hold declarations, `.cpp` files hold definitions.

By default arguments are passed **by value**: the parameter is a copy, so changes inside the function don't affect the caller. Copying an `int` is free, but copying a large `std::vector` or `std::string` is not; the next lessons show how references avoid that.

A few modern touches:

- `auto f(int x) { return x * 2; }` deduces the return type from the `return` statement.
- Trailing return syntax `auto f(int x) -> int` is equivalent and common in generic code.
- `[[nodiscard]] int parse(...)` makes the compiler warn when the caller ignores the result, which is great for error codes.

Recursion works as you'd expect, but each call uses stack space, so very deep recursion can overflow the stack.

Keep functions short and give them one job. A function you can describe in one sentence is easy to test, and the compiler inlines small functions, so splitting code up costs nothing at run time.
takeaways: Declare before use; a prototype is enough, the definition can come later or elsewhere
Arguments are copied by default
Mark results callers must check with `[[nodiscard]]`
pitfalls: Forgetting to return a value on some path of a non-void function — it compiles but is undefined behaviour.

quiz.q: `void reset(int n) { n = 0; }` is called as `reset(count);`. What happens to count?
options: Nothing; reset changed its own copy
Compile error: n is not a reference
quiz.explain: Parameters are passed by value, so only the local copy n is set to 0.

quiz.q: main calls helper(), which is defined further down the file with no earlier declaration. What happens?
options: The compiler reports that helper was not declared
The linker reports an undefined reference
It compiles; the compiler scans the whole file first
quiz.explain: Names must be declared before use within a translation unit; add a prototype above main.

concepts.name: Overloading and default arguments
concepts.summary: Give several functions the same name with different parameter types, and make trailing parameters optional with defaults.
concepts.why: Overloading is everywhere in the standard library and is the basis for operator overloading and templates.
concepts.body:
C++ lets several functions share a name as long as their parameter lists differ. At each call the compiler picks the best match by **overload resolution**: an exact match beats a promotion (like `char` to `int` or `float` to `double`), which beats a standard conversion (like `int` to `double`), which beats a user-defined conversion (like `const char*` to `std::string`).

Overloads differ by parameters only. Two functions that differ only in return type can't coexist, because the call `f(1)` wouldn't tell them apart.

If two candidates are equally good, the call is **ambiguous** and won't compile. A classic example is calling `print(3L)` when only `print(int)` and `print(double)` exist: converting `long` to either is a standard conversion, so neither wins. The fix is an explicit cast or another overload.

Overloading on `T` versus `const T&` for the same type is usually ambiguous too, so pick one parameter style per type.

**Default arguments** make trailing parameters optional: `pad(std::string s, std::size_t width = 8, char fill = '.')` can be called with one, two or three arguments. Defaults must come at the end of the list, and they belong in the declaration that callers see (usually the header), not repeated in the definition.

Use overloading when the functions do the same thing for different types (like `std::to_string`). If the behaviour differs, give them different names. Prefer a default argument over a second overload when only one value changes. Templates, covered later, write the overloads for you when the code is identical for every type.
takeaways: Overloads must differ in parameters, never only in return type
Exact match > promotion > conversion > user-defined conversion; ties are errors
Default arguments go at the end, in the declaration
pitfalls: Repeating the default value in both the header declaration and the .cpp definition — that's a compile error.

quiz.q: Given only `void f(long)` and `void f(double)`, what does `f(5)` do?
options: It is ambiguous and does not compile
quiz.explain: int to long and int to double are both standard conversions of equal rank, so neither overload is better.

quiz.q: Which declaration is valid?
options: void g(int a = 1, int a2 = a);
int g(int a); double g(int a);
quiz.explain: Defaults must be trailing; overloads can't differ only in return type, and a default can't use another parameter.

concepts.name: References
concepts.summary: Use references as aliases to pass large objects without copying and to let functions modify their arguments.
concepts.why: Pass-by-const-reference is the default way to hand objects to functions in C++, and references appear in almost every signature.
concepts.body:
A **reference** is another name for an existing object. `int& r = a;` makes `r` an alias of `a`: reading or writing `r` reads or writes `a`. A reference must be initialized when it's declared and can never be rebound. `r = b;` doesn't make `r` refer to `b`; it assigns `b`'s value to `a`.

References are mostly used in function parameters:

- `void f(T& x)`: the function works on the caller's object and may modify it ("out" or "in-out" parameter).
- `void f(const T& x)`: no copy and no modification. This is the standard way to pass anything bigger than a few machine words, such as strings, vectors and user types. A const reference can also bind to temporaries: `f(std::string{"tmp"})` works.
- `void f(T x)`: by value, for cheap types like `int`, `double` and small structs, or when the function needs its own copy anyway.

In range-for loops, `for (auto& x : v)` lets you modify elements and `for (const auto& x : v)` reads them without copying.

The big danger is a **dangling reference**: a reference that outlives the object it refers to. Returning a reference to a local variable is the classic case; the local is destroyed when the function returns, and using the reference is undefined behaviour. Compilers warn about the obvious cases but not all of them. Returning a reference is fine when the object lives on, such as a member of `*this` or an element of a container the caller owns.

Unlike pointers, references can't be null and need no special syntax to use, which makes them the default choice for "refer to an object that definitely exists".
takeaways: A reference is an alias: must be initialised, can't be null, can't be rebound
Pass big objects as `const T&`, outputs as `T&`, small values by value
Never return a reference to a local variable
pitfalls: Returning a reference (or `std::string_view`) to a local or temporary that is destroyed at the end of the function.

quiz.q: After `int x = 1, y = 5; int& r = x; r = y; y = 9;`, what is x?
quiz.explain: r = y copies y's value (5) into x; r still refers to x, so the later change to y doesn't matter.

quiz.q: Which signature is the idiomatic way to pass a large std::vector that the function only reads?
quiz.explain: A const reference avoids the copy and documents that the function won't modify the argument.

concepts.name: Arrays and std::vector
concepts.summary: Store sequences of values: built-in arrays, fixed-size std::array, and std::vector, the dynamic array you should reach for first.
concepts.why: std::vector is the most-used container in C++; it is the right default for almost any list of things.
concepts.body:
C++ inherited **built-in arrays** from C: `int a[3] = {1, 2, 3};`. Their size is fixed at compile time, they don't know their own size when passed to a function (they decay to a pointer), they can't be assigned, and `a[10]` is not checked. Modern code rarely uses them directly.

`std::array<int, 3>` (header `<array>`) is a fixed-size array with no overhead that behaves like a proper value: it knows its `size()`, can be copied and compared, and works with the standard algorithms.

`std::vector<T>` (header `<vector>`) is a **dynamic array**: elements sit contiguously in heap memory and the vector grows as needed.

- `push_back(x)` appends; `emplace_back(args...)` constructs the element in place; `pop_back()` removes the last one.
- `size()`, `empty()`, `front()`, `back()`, `clear()`.
- `v[i]` is unchecked (out of range is undefined behaviour); `v.at(i)` checks and throws `std::out_of_range`.
- `reserve(n)` preallocates capacity when you know roughly how many elements are coming, avoiding repeated reallocations.

When a vector runs out of capacity it allocates a bigger block (typically 1.5x or 2x), moves the elements over and frees the old block. Appends are therefore cheap on average, but any pointers, references or iterators to elements become invalid after a reallocation. Don't hold on to `&v[0]` across a `push_back`.

Contiguous storage is why `std::vector` is so fast: iteration is cache-friendly and the CPU prefetches well. Even when you insert in the middle now and then, a vector usually beats a linked list. Make it your default container.
takeaways: `std::vector` is the default container: contiguous, fast, growable
`v[i]` is unchecked, `v.at(i)` throws on a bad index
Growth reallocates and invalidates pointers, references and iterators to elements
pitfalls: Keeping a reference or pointer to an element and then calling `push_back`, which may reallocate and leave it dangling.

quiz.q: A vector has size() == 4 and capacity() == 4. You hold `int& first = v[0];` and call `v.push_back(5);`. What about first?
options: push_back throws because capacity is full
It refers to the new element
It may now dangle, because the elements were probably moved to a new block
quiz.explain: A full vector must reallocate to grow, which invalidates all references to its old elements.

quiz.q: Which of these knows its size at compile time and can be copied with `=`?
quiz.explain: std::array has a compile-time size and value semantics; a built-in array can't be assigned and a vector's size is dynamic.

concepts.name: std::string and string_view
concepts.summary: Work with text using std::string, and pass read-only text cheaply with std::string_view.
concepts.why: Text processing is everywhere, and choosing between string, string_view and C strings affects both safety and speed.
concepts.body:
`std::string` (header `<string>`) owns a mutable sequence of `char`s and manages its own memory. It behaves like a value: copying a string copies its characters, and `==` compares contents.

The common operations:

- Concatenate with `+` and `+=`; `size()` and `empty()`; index with `s[i]`.
- `s.substr(pos, count)` copies out a piece; `s.find("x")` returns a position or `std::string::npos` if not found.
- C++20 adds `starts_with` and `ends_with`; C++23 adds `contains`.
- Convert with `std::to_string(42)` and `std::stoi("42")` / `std::stod` (these throw on bad input).

A string literal like `"abc"` is not a `std::string`; it's a `const char[4]` array inherited from C, with a hidden terminating `'\0'`. So `"a" + "b"` doesn't compile (it tries to add two pointers), while `std::string{"a"} + "b"` works. Short strings (typically up to 15 characters) are stored inside the string object itself, the **small string optimization**, so they don't allocate.

`std::string_view` (C++17, header `<string_view>`) is a non-owning view: just a pointer and a length. It can refer to a `std::string`, a literal or part of a buffer without copying, which makes `std::string_view` the best parameter type for functions that only read text. Its `substr` is free.

The flip side: a view does not keep the text alive. Never return a `string_view` into a local string, and never store one that outlives the string it points to.

`char` holds bytes, not Unicode characters; UTF-8 text works fine in a `std::string`, but `size()` counts bytes.
takeaways: `std::string` owns its text; `std::string_view` only looks at someone else's
Take read-only text parameters as `std::string_view`
`find` returns `std::string::npos` when nothing matches
pitfalls: Returning a `std::string_view` that points into a local or temporary `std::string`.

quiz.q: Why doesn't `auto s = "Hello, " + "world";` compile?
options: String literals are const char arrays, and adding two pointers is not allowed
operator+ is only defined for std::string_view
quiz.explain: Neither operand is a std::string, so no string operator+ applies; the arrays decay to pointers that can't be added.

quiz.q: Which parameter type lets a read-only function accept a std::string, a literal, or part of a buffer without copying?
quiz.explain: string_view is a pointer-plus-length view that binds to all of these without allocating.

concepts.name: Structs and classes
concepts.summary: Group data and behaviour into your own types with struct and class, member functions and public/private access.
concepts.why: User-defined types are how C++ programs model their domain, and the class is the foundation for RAII and the rest of the language.
concepts.body:
A `struct` or `class` defines a new type that groups data members and member functions. The only difference between the two keywords is the default access: members of a `struct` are public by default, members of a `class` are private. By convention, use `struct` for plain bundles of data and `class` for types that protect an **invariant**, a rule that must always hold, such as "balance is never changed except through deposit".

- Data members can have default values: `double x = 0;`.
- Member functions see the members directly; inside them `this` points to the current object.
- A member function marked `const` after its parameter list promises not to modify the object, and is the only kind you can call on a const object.
- `public:` and `private:` sections control who can touch what. Keep data private and expose operations, so the class can check every change.

A struct with only public data and no constructors is an **aggregate**, initialized with braces in member order: `Point p{1.5, 2.0};`. C++20 adds **designated initializers**, `Point q{.x = 3, .y = 4};`, which must follow declaration order but can skip members, which keep their defaults.

Classes with invariants use a **constructor**, a member function with the class's name that runs when the object is created, to establish them. Mark single-argument constructors `explicit` so a plain `std::string` can't silently convert into an `Account`.

Objects are values: `Point b = a;` copies all members, and each object has its own data. Member functions don't add to an object's size; only data members do.
takeaways: `struct` and `class` differ only in default access
Keep data private when the type has an invariant; expose operations
Aggregates take `{...}` initialisation; C++20 adds `.member = value`
pitfalls: Making every member public with getters and setters for each — that protects nothing; expose meaningful operations instead.

quiz.q: What is the only language difference between `struct S { int a; };` and `class S { int a; };`?
options: A class can have member functions, a struct cannot
Structs are allocated on the stack, classes on the heap
Members are public by default in a struct and private in a class
quiz.explain: Both keywords define the same kind of type; only the default access (and default base access) differ.

quiz.q: Why mark `long balance() const`?
options: It prevents derived classes from overriding it
It lets it be called on const objects and promises not to modify the object
It makes the return value const
quiz.explain: A const member function can be called through const references and can't change the object's members.

concepts.name: Constructors, destructors and RAII
concepts.summary: Initialise objects with constructors, clean up with destructors, and tie every resource to an object's lifetime (RAII).
concepts.why: RAII is the central idiom of C++: it is how the language manages memory, files and locks without a garbage collector or finally blocks.
concepts.body:
A **constructor** runs when an object is created and a **destructor** (`~T()`) runs when it is destroyed. For a local variable that happens deterministically: at the closing brace of its scope, in reverse order of construction, including when the scope is left by `return`, `break` or an exception.

Initialize members in the **member initializer list**, `Trace(std::string n) : name_{std::move(n)} {}`, not by assigning in the body. Members are always initialized in the order they are declared in the class, whatever order you write the list in, so keep the two consistent (`-Wall` warns otherwise). `const` members and reference members can only be set there.

Other constructor tools:

- `T() = default;` keeps the compiler-generated default constructor; one constructor can delegate to another: `T() : T(0) {}`.
- `explicit` on single-argument constructors prevents surprising implicit conversions.

**RAII** ("Resource Acquisition Is Initialization") means: acquire a resource in a constructor, release it in the destructor. The resource can be heap memory, a file handle, a socket, a mutex lock or a database transaction. Because destructors always run when the owning object goes away, the resource can't leak, even on error paths. You get cleanup with no `finally` and no manual `close()` calls.

The standard library is built this way: `std::vector` and `std::string` free their memory, `std::ofstream` closes its file, `std::lock_guard` unlocks its mutex, and `std::unique_ptr` deletes its object.

The rule of thumb: never manage a resource manually in application code. Wrap it in a class (or use an existing one), and let scope do the cleanup. Destructors must not throw; they are implicitly `noexcept`.
takeaways: Destructors run at scope exit in reverse order, on every path including exceptions
RAII: acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor
Members are initialised in declaration order; use the member initializer list
pitfalls: Writing a member initializer list in a different order than the declarations and reading a member before it is initialised.

quiz.q: A function creates `A a; B b; C c;` and then throws. In what order are they destroyed?
options: They are not destroyed because of the exception
quiz.explain: Stack unwinding destroys fully constructed locals in reverse order of construction.

quiz.q: Class X declares `int a; int b;` and its constructor is `X() : b{1}, a{b + 1} {}`. What is wrong?
options: a is initialised first, reading b before b is initialised
b must be listed first in the class
Initializer lists can't use other members
quiz.explain: Members initialise in declaration order, so a{b + 1} runs while b is still uninitialised.

concepts.name: Const correctness
concepts.summary: Mark what must not change with const: variables, reference parameters and member functions, so the compiler enforces it.
concepts.why: Const is a contract the compiler checks; const-correct interfaces are safer, clearer, and required to work with const objects.
concepts.body:
`const` says "this won't change", and the compiler holds you to it. It appears in three main places.

**Const variables.** `const int max_items = 10;` can't be modified after initialization. Use it by default for values you don't intend to change; it makes code easier to reason about. (For values known at compile time, `constexpr` is even stronger; see the Advanced lessons.)

**Const references and pointers in parameters.** `void report(const Inventory& inv)` promises the caller that `inv` won't be modified, and it accepts temporaries and const objects. For pointers, read right to left: `const int* p` is a pointer to a const int (can't change `*p`, can repoint `p`), while `int* const p` is a const pointer to a mutable int.

**Const member functions.** `std::size_t count() const;` means the function doesn't modify the object. Only const member functions can be called on a const object or through a const reference. That makes const contagious in a good way: if `count()` forgets its `const`, nobody holding a `const Inventory&` can call it. Mark every member function that doesn't change observable state as const.

Getters often come in a pair, a const version returning `const T&` and a non-const version returning `T&`, as `std::vector::operator[]` does.

Sometimes a const function needs to update something that isn't part of the object's logical state: a cache, a statistics counter or a mutex. Declare such members `mutable`. Use it sparingly, and remember a const function may be called from several threads at once, so mutable state needs synchronization.

Avoid `const_cast` to strip const; modifying an object that was defined const is undefined behaviour.
takeaways: Mark every member function that doesn't change the object `const`
`const int*` = pointer to const; `int* const` = const pointer
`mutable` is for caches and counters, not for real state
pitfalls: Forgetting `const` on a getter, which makes it uncallable through every `const&` in the codebase.

quiz.q: `void show(const Widget& w) { w.draw(); }` fails to compile. What is the most likely fix?
options: Change the parameter to Widget w
Declare draw() as a const member function
quiz.explain: Through a const reference only const member functions can be called, so draw() needs to be const if it doesn't modify the widget.

quiz.q: Given `int a = 1, b = 2; const int* p = &a;`, which statement compiles?
quiz.explain: p points to const int, so the pointee can't be modified through p, but p itself can be repointed.

concepts.name: Pointers
concepts.summary: Understand raw pointers: addresses, dereferencing, nullptr, pointer arithmetic, and their modern role as non-owning observers.
concepts.why: Pointers underlie arrays, polymorphism, data structures and every C API, and you must read them fluently even if you rarely own memory with them.
concepts.body:
A **pointer** holds the address of an object. `int* p = &x;` stores the address of `x`; `*p` dereferences it to reach `x`. For a pointer to a struct, `p->member` is shorthand for `(*p).member`.

Unlike references, pointers can be **null** (`nullptr`, never `NULL` or `0` in modern code), can be reassigned to point elsewhere, and need explicit dereferencing. Dereferencing a null or dangling pointer is undefined behaviour, so check for `nullptr` wherever null is a valid state.

Pointers and arrays are closely tied. An array name **decays** to a pointer to its first element, and **pointer arithmetic** moves by whole elements: `p + 2` points two `int`s further, and `p[i]` means `*(p + i)`. Arithmetic is only valid within one array (plus one past the end); going beyond is undefined.

`const` applies as usual, read right to left: `const T*` can't modify the pointee, `T* const` can't be repointed.

You can allocate with `new` and must then `delete` (or `new[]` with `delete[]`). Doing this by hand leaks memory on early returns and exceptions and invites double deletes. In modern C++ **raw pointers don't own**: use containers and smart pointers for ownership, and use raw pointers (or references) only to observe objects someone else owns.

So when should a function take `T*` instead of `T&`? When "no object" is a valid argument. Otherwise a reference states the intent better. Raw pointers remain essential for linked structures that point to optional neighbours, for C APIs, and for low-level code.
takeaways: `&x` takes an address, `*p` dereferences, `p->m` accesses a member
Use `nullptr`; dereferencing null or a dangling pointer is undefined behaviour
Raw pointers observe; containers and smart pointers own
pitfalls: Using `new`/`delete` by hand in application code, leaking on early return or exception.

quiz.explain: p points at a[1], so p[2] is *(p + 2), which is a[3] = 40.

quiz.q: When is a raw `T*` parameter more appropriate than `T&`?
options: When passing "no object" (nullptr) is a valid option
When the function needs to modify the object
quiz.explain: References can't be null, so a pointer expresses an optional argument; ownership transfer should use a smart pointer.

concepts.name: Smart pointers
concepts.summary: Own heap objects safely with std::unique_ptr, share them with std::shared_ptr, and break cycles with std::weak_ptr.
concepts.why: Smart pointers make heap ownership explicit and leak-free; they replace almost every use of new and delete.
concepts.body:
Smart pointers (header `<memory>`) are RAII classes that own a heap object and delete it automatically.

`std::unique_ptr<T>` is **sole ownership**. Create it with `std::make_unique<T>(args...)`. It can't be copied, only moved, so ownership transfers are visible in the code: `auto b = std::move(a);` leaves `a` null. It has no overhead over a raw pointer, which makes it the default choice. It also handles arrays (`std::unique_ptr<int[]>`) and custom deleters, for example to `fclose` a `FILE*`.

`std::shared_ptr<T>` is **shared ownership** with reference counting: each copy increments a count, and the object is deleted when the last `shared_ptr` goes away. Create it with `std::make_shared<T>(args...)`, which puts the object and its control block in one allocation. The count is updated atomically, so it's safe to copy shared pointers across threads (the pointed-to object itself is not synchronized). Copying costs an atomic increment, so pass `shared_ptr` by reference or don't pass it at all when the callee doesn't need ownership.

`std::weak_ptr<T>` observes a shared object without keeping it alive. Call `lock()` to get a `shared_ptr` if the object still exists. Use it to break **cycles**: two objects holding `shared_ptr`s to each other never reach a count of zero and leak.

Guidelines:

- Prefer `unique_ptr`; reach for `shared_ptr` only when ownership is genuinely shared.
- Functions that just use an object should take `T&` or `T*`, not a smart pointer.
- Never construct two smart pointers from the same raw pointer: each would delete it.
takeaways: `unique_ptr` by default: zero overhead, move-only ownership
`shared_ptr` for genuinely shared ownership; `weak_ptr` to observe and break cycles
Create with `make_unique` / `make_shared`; pass `T&` to functions that don't own
pitfalls: Two objects holding `shared_ptr`s to each other: the cycle keeps both alive forever. Make one side a `weak_ptr`.

quiz.q: What happens with `auto a = std::make_unique<int>(5); auto b = a;`?
options: b gets a deep copy of the int
Compile error: unique_ptr can't be copied
quiz.explain: unique_ptr's copy constructor is deleted; you must write std::move(a) to transfer ownership.

quiz.q: A function only reads a Texture and doesn't care how it's owned. What should it take?
quiz.explain: Taking a reference works with any ownership scheme and costs nothing; smart pointer parameters imply ownership.

concepts.name: Inheritance and virtual functions
concepts.summary: Build class hierarchies with public inheritance, override virtual functions for runtime polymorphism, and use virtual destructors.
concepts.why: Runtime polymorphism through virtual functions is how C++ code handles plugin-style designs, GUI widgets and many frameworks.
concepts.body:
`class Circle : public Shape` makes `Circle` a `Shape`: it inherits Shape's members, and a `Circle` can be used wherever a `Shape&` or `Shape*` is expected.

A member function declared `virtual` in the base is dispatched at run time on the object's real type. Calling `s->area()` through a `Shape*` that points to a `Circle` runs `Circle::area`. Mark each overriding function `override`: the compiler then errors if the signature doesn't actually match a base virtual, which catches typos and mismatched `const`. A function declared `= 0` is **pure virtual**; a class with one is **abstract** and can't be instantiated, which makes it an interface. `final` stops further overriding or derivation.

Three rules that matter in practice:

- Give a polymorphic base class a **virtual destructor** (`virtual ~Shape() = default;`). Otherwise deleting a derived object through a base pointer, which is exactly what `std::unique_ptr<Shape>` does, is undefined behaviour.
- Polymorphism only works through references and pointers. Copying a `Circle` into a `Shape` variable **slices** it: only the base part is copied and the virtual calls go to `Shape`. Hold polymorphic objects as `std::unique_ptr<Base>` in containers.
- Don't call virtual functions from constructors or destructors expecting derived behaviour; during construction the object is still only a base.

Each polymorphic object carries a hidden pointer to its class's vtable, and a virtual call is an indirect call that's hard to inline. That cost is small but real in hot loops.

Use inheritance for "is-a" relationships with polymorphic behaviour. To reuse code, prefer composition (a member) over inheritance.
takeaways: `virtual` + `override` gives runtime dispatch; always write `override`
Polymorphic bases need a virtual destructor
Use polymorphic objects through references or pointers; copying slices them
pitfalls: Storing derived objects in a `std::vector<Base>` — they are sliced to Base. Use `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Base>>`.

quiz.q: `Shape s = Circle{2.0}; s.name();` — Shape::name is virtual and Circle overrides it. Which runs? (Assume Shape is not abstract.)
options: Shape::name, because s is a sliced Shape object
quiz.explain: Assigning to a Shape value copies only the base part, so s really is a Shape and calls Shape::name.

quiz.q: Why does the base class need `virtual ~Shape()` when shapes are held as `std::unique_ptr<Shape>`?
options: Without it, deleting a Circle through a Shape* is undefined behaviour
unique_ptr requires every class to have a virtual destructor
It's only needed if Circle has a destructor
quiz.explain: unique_ptr<Shape> deletes through Shape*, which only calls the derived destructor correctly if the base destructor is virtual.

concepts.name: Operator overloading
concepts.summary: Give your types natural syntax: arithmetic, comparisons with C++20's spaceship operator, and stream output.
concepts.why: Well-chosen operators make value types like money, vectors or dates read like built-ins, and the standard library relies on them.
concepts.body:
You can define what operators mean for your own types by writing functions named `operator+`, `operator==`, `operator<<` and so on. The rule is to keep the usual meaning: `+` should add, `==` should compare, and nothing should surprise the reader.

Some conventions:

- Implement compound assignment (`+=`) as a member returning `*this` by reference, then write `+` in terms of it.
- Make symmetric binary operators non-members, so conversions apply to both operands. A popular way is a **hidden friend**: a `friend` function defined inside the class body, found only by argument-dependent lookup.
- Stream output is always a non-member: `std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const T& v)`, returning `os` so calls chain.
- Other common ones: `operator[]` for indexing (C++23 allows several arguments), `operator()` to make function objects, and `operator bool` (declare it `explicit`).

C++20 transformed comparisons. Declare `auto operator<=>(const T&) const = default;` (the **three-way comparison** or "spaceship" operator) and the compiler compares members in declaration order and gives you `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. A defaulted `<=>` also implicitly declares a defaulted `operator==`, so you get `==` and `!=` too. If you write `<=>` by hand, also define `==` yourself, since equality is often cheaper to compute than ordering. The result is a `std::strong_ordering` (or `weak_ordering`/`partial_ordering` for doubles), from `<compare>`.

The compiler also rewrites expressions: `a != b` uses `operator==`, and `b < a` can be served by `a <=> b`. That removes the old boilerplate of writing six comparison operators.

Don't overload `&&`, `||` or `,`: overloaded versions lose short-circuiting and ordering guarantees.
takeaways: Keep the conventional meaning of each operator
Write `+=` as a member, `+` (and `<<`) as non-member or hidden friend
C++20: a defaulted `<=>` gives all six comparisons
pitfalls: Writing a custom `operator<=>` and expecting `==` to appear — only a *defaulted* `<=>` declares `==` for you.

quiz.q: A struct declares only `auto operator<=>(const P&) const = default;`. Which expressions compile?
quiz.explain: A defaulted <=> also implicitly declares a defaulted ==, and != is rewritten in terms of ==.

quiz.q: Why is `operator<<` for printing written as a non-member?
options: Its left operand is the std::ostream, which isn't your class
quiz.explain: A member operator always has the class object as its left operand, but in `std::cout << x` the left operand is the stream.

concepts.name: Scoped enums (enum class)
concepts.summary: Define named sets of constants with enum class, which are scoped, strongly typed and can choose their underlying type.
concepts.why: Enums replace magic numbers and bool parameters; enum class does it without the name clashes and silent conversions of old enums.
concepts.body:
An enumeration is a type with a fixed set of named values. C++ has two kinds.

The old C-style `enum Color { Red, Green };` puts `Red` and `Green` directly into the surrounding scope (so two enums can't both have `None`) and converts silently to `int`, so `Red + 3` and `if (color == 1)` compile.

The C++11 **scoped enum**, `enum class Level { Debug, Info, Warn, Error };`, fixes both problems:

- Values are scoped: you write `Level::Warn`.
- No implicit conversion to integers; use `static_cast<int>(l)` when you need the number, or C++23's `std::to_underlying(l)`.
- Comparisons between values of the same enum still work: `l >= Level::Warn`.

You can fix the underlying type, `enum class Level : std::uint8_t`, to control size in structs and binary formats; for scoped enums it defaults to `int`. Values count up from 0 unless you assign them explicitly (`Error = 40`). Enums with a specified underlying type can be forward-declared.

`switch` on an enum is the natural way to handle each case. If the switch has no `default`, `-Wall` warns when you forget an enumerator, which is a useful safety net when someone adds a new value later. C++20's `using enum Level;` brings the names into a scope so you can write `case Warn:` instead of `case Level::Warn:`.

Use enum class for states, modes and options instead of `int` codes or several `bool` parameters: `open(path, Mode::ReadOnly)` reads far better than `open(path, true, false)`. There's still no built-in enum-to-string conversion; write a function with a switch.
takeaways: Prefer `enum class`: scoped names, no implicit int conversion
Choose the underlying type with `: std::uint8_t` when size matters
Switch without `default` so the compiler flags missing cases
pitfalls: Adding a `default:` to every enum switch, which silences the warning that would tell you about a newly added enumerator.

quiz.q: Given `enum class Dir { Up, Down };`, which line compiles?
quiz.explain: Scoped enum values compare with each other, but don't convert to or from int and need the Dir:: prefix.

quiz.q: Why might you write `enum class Opcode : std::uint8_t`?
options: To make each Opcode exactly one byte, e.g. in a packed message
To allow implicit conversion to uint8_t
To make the values start at 1
It is required for switch statements
quiz.explain: The underlying type fixes the storage size; conversions still need an explicit cast.

concepts.name: Standard containers
concepts.summary: Choose between vector, deque, map, set, unordered_map and friends, and use their lookup and insertion APIs correctly.
concepts.why: Picking the right container is the most common design decision in C++ code and has a big effect on speed and clarity.
concepts.body:
The standard library's containers fall into a few families:

- **Sequence**: `std::vector` (the default), `std::array` (fixed size), `std::deque` (fast push/pop at both ends), `std::list` / `std::forward_list` (linked lists, rarely the right choice).
- **Ordered associative**: `std::map<K, V>` and `std::set<K>`, kept sorted by key in a balanced tree. Lookup, insert and erase are O(log n), and iteration is in key order.
- **Unordered associative**: `std::unordered_map` and `std::unordered_set`, hash tables with average O(1) operations and no ordering. Keys need `std::hash` and `==`.
- **Adapters**: `std::stack`, `std::queue`, `std::priority_queue` (a heap) on top of another container.

Map APIs have well-known traps. `m[key]` inserts a default-constructed value if the key is missing, which is convenient for counting (`++freq[word]`) but surprising for lookups, and unavailable on a const map. To look up without inserting, use `find` (returns `end()` when missing), `contains` (C++20) or `at` (throws). `try_emplace` and `insert_or_assign` are the clear way to insert. Iterate with structured bindings: `for (const auto& [key, value] : m)`.

Rules of thumb: start with `vector`; use `unordered_map` for fast key lookup; use `map` when you need sorted order or range queries like `lower_bound`. For a small, mostly-read lookup table, a sorted vector often beats both thanks to cache locality; C++23 packages that idea as `std::flat_map` and `std::flat_set`.

All containers are RAII values: they free everything they hold, copy deeply and can be moved cheaply.
takeaways: `vector` first; `unordered_map` for fast lookup; `map` for sorted keys
`m[k]` inserts when k is missing — use `find`, `contains` or `at` to look up
Iterate maps with `for (const auto& [k, v] : m)`
pitfalls: Using `if (m[key] == 0)` to test for presence, which inserts every key you test.

quiz.q: You need to print all entries sorted by key and occasionally find all keys in a range. Which container fits best?
quiz.explain: std::map keeps keys sorted, so in-order iteration and lower_bound/upper_bound range queries are natural.

quiz.q: After `std::map<std::string, int> m; if (m["a"] > 0) {}`, what is m.size()?
quiz.explain: operator[] inserts a value-initialised entry for a missing key, so "a" is now in the map with value 0.

concepts.name: Iterators
concepts.summary: Traverse any container with iterators, understand half-open ranges and iterator categories, and avoid invalidation bugs.
concepts.why: Iterators are the glue between containers and algorithms; misusing an invalidated iterator is one of the most common C++ bugs.
concepts.body:
An **iterator** is a generalised pointer into a container: `*it` gives the element, `++it` advances. Every container has `begin()`, pointing at the first element, and `end()`, pointing **one past the last**. Ranges are half-open, `[begin, end)`, so an empty container has `begin() == end()` and loops use `it != end()`.

Range-for is built on these: `for (auto x : v)` is shorthand for a loop from `begin()` to `end()`. Other variations are `cbegin()` for read-only iteration and `rbegin()`/`rend()` for reverse order.

Iterators come in **categories** that determine which algorithms they work with:

- Input/forward: only `++` (e.g. `std::forward_list`, stream iterators).
- Bidirectional: `++` and `--` (`std::list`, `std::map`, `std::set`).
- Random access: also `it + n`, `it[n]`, `it2 - it1` (`std::deque`).
- Contiguous: random access with elements adjacent in memory (`std::vector`, `std::array`, `std::string`).

That's why `std::sort` works on a vector but not on a list (which has its own `sort()` member).

The critical rule is **invalidation**. Operations that change a container's structure can invalidate iterators, pointers and references into it. For `std::vector`, any reallocation invalidates everything, and `erase` invalidates everything from the erased point on. Node-based containers (`list`, `map`, `set`) only invalidate iterators to erased elements. Using an invalid iterator is undefined behaviour.

To erase while iterating, use the iterator that `erase` returns. Better still, C++20's `std::erase(v, value)` and `std::erase_if(v, pred)` remove matching elements in one call.
takeaways: Ranges are half-open: `[begin(), end())`; `end()` is never dereferenced
Iterator category decides which algorithms apply (e.g. `std::sort` needs random access)
Structural changes can invalidate iterators; continue from the one `erase` returns
pitfalls: Calling `v.erase(it)` inside a for loop and then doing `++it` on the invalidated iterator.

quiz.q: Which container's iterators allow `it + 5`?
quiz.explain: deque iterators are random access; list and map are bidirectional and forward_list is forward-only.

quiz.q: You hold an iterator to the 2nd element of a vector and then erase the 1st element. What about your iterator?
options: Invalidated: erase invalidates iterators at or after the erased position
Still valid, pointing at the same value
Automatically moved to the new 1st element
Valid only if capacity didn't change
quiz.explain: vector::erase shifts later elements down, so iterators from the erase point onwards are invalidated.

concepts.name: Lambdas
concepts.summary: Write inline function objects with lambdas: captures by value and by reference, generic lambdas, and storing callables.
concepts.why: Lambdas are how you customise algorithms, write callbacks and launch threads in modern C++.
concepts.body:
A **lambda** is an anonymous function object written inline: `[captures](params) { body }`. The return type is deduced, or given as `-> T`.

The capture list says which outside variables the lambda can use:

- `[x]` copies `x` into the lambda when it's created; `[&x]` refers to the original.
- `[=]` and `[&]` capture everything used, by copy or by reference. Prefer listing captures explicitly in longer code.
- Init-captures create new members: `[n = 0]`, or `[p = std::move(ptr)]` to move a unique_ptr in.
- In a member function, `[this]` captures the object pointer and `[*this]` copies the object.

Captured copies are const inside the lambda unless you mark it `mutable`, which lets a lambda keep its own state between calls.

Each lambda has its own unique, unnamed type, so store one in `auto`. With `auto` parameters you get a **generic lambda**, a template in disguise; C++20 also allows an explicit template parameter list, `[]<typename T>(T x) { ... }`. Lambdas with no captures convert to plain function pointers, handy for C APIs.

To store different callables in one variable or container, such as a list of callbacks, use `std::function<int(int)>` from `<functional>`. It type-erases any callable with that signature, at the cost of a possible heap allocation and an indirect call. Templates or `auto` parameters avoid that cost when you just pass a lambda to a function. C++23 adds `std::move_only_function` for callables that can't be copied.

The main danger: a lambda that captures by reference must not outlive the variables it captured. That bites with callbacks, threads and lambdas returned from functions; capture by value there.
takeaways: `[x]` copies at creation, `[&x]` refers to the live variable
Use `mutable` to modify by-value captures; init-captures `[p = std::move(x)]` move things in
`std::function` stores any callable but costs more than `auto`/templates
pitfalls: Capturing locals by reference in a callback or thread that runs after the function has returned.

quiz.q: What does this print? `int x = 1; auto f = [x] { return x; }; x = 5; std::cout << f();`
quiz.explain: A by-value capture copies x when the lambda is created, so later changes to x are not seen.

quiz.q: Why does `[n = 0]() { return ++n; }` fail to compile?
options: By-value captures are const unless the lambda is mutable
quiz.explain: The lambda's call operator is const by default, so modifying a captured copy requires `mutable`.

concepts.name: Standard algorithms
concepts.summary: Replace hand-written loops with std::sort, find_if, transform, accumulate and the rest of <algorithm> and <numeric>.
concepts.why: Named algorithms are clearer, tested and often faster than raw loops, and every C++ reviewer expects you to know them.
concepts.body:
The headers `<algorithm>` and `<numeric>` hold over a hundred generic algorithms that operate on iterator ranges, usually customised with a lambda. Knowing the common ones turns ten-line loops into one line that states its intent.

- Searching: `find`, `find_if`, `any_of`/`all_of`/`none_of`, `count_if`, and on sorted ranges `binary_search`, `lower_bound`, `equal_range`.
- Sorting: `sort` (not stable), `stable_sort`, `partial_sort`, `nth_element` (k-th element in O(n)), `is_sorted`.
- Transforming: `transform`, `copy_if`, `fill`, `iota`, `reverse`, `rotate`, `unique`.
- Reducing: `accumulate` and `reduce` (`<numeric>`), `min_element`, `max_element`, `minmax_element`.

Comparators must define a **strict weak ordering**: use `<`, never `<=`, or `std::sort` can misbehave and even crash.

Algorithms never change the size of a container, since they only see iterators. `remove_if` and `unique` move kept elements to the front and return the new logical end; you must then call `erase` to shrink the container (the **erase-remove idiom**). For the remove case, C++20's `std::erase_if` does both steps.

Watch `accumulate`'s initial value: its type is the type of the accumulator, so `accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0)` over doubles truncates every step to `int`. Pass `0.0`.

Output algorithms like `transform` and `copy` write to an output iterator and assume there's room: size the destination first or use `std::back_inserter(dest)`.

Since C++17, many algorithms accept an execution policy such as `std::execution::par` to run in parallel. The C++20 range versions in the Advanced lessons take whole containers instead of iterator pairs.
takeaways: Prefer a named algorithm to a raw loop: it states intent
`remove_if`/`unique` don't shrink the container — follow with `erase` (or use `std::erase_if`)
Comparators must be strict (`<`), and `accumulate`'s initial value sets the result type
pitfalls: Passing `0` instead of `0.0` to `std::accumulate` over doubles, silently truncating the sum.

quiz.q: v is {1, 2, 3, 2} and you call `std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), 2);` without erase. What is v.size() afterwards?
quiz.explain: Algorithms can't change a container's size; remove only shuffles kept elements forward and returns the new logical end.

quiz.q: What's wrong with `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a <= b; });`?
options: <= is not a strict weak ordering, so the behaviour is undefined
quiz.explain: Comparators must return false for equal elements; <= breaks that and can make sort read out of bounds.

concepts.name: Headers, namespaces and the ODR
concepts.summary: Split code into headers and source files, organise names with namespaces, and follow the one-definition rule.
concepts.why: Every multi-file C++ project depends on this structure, and most linker errors come from getting it wrong.
concepts.body:
C++ code is split into **headers** (`.h`/`.hpp`), which contain declarations other files need, and **source files** (`.cpp`), which contain definitions. A source file `#include`s the headers it uses; the preprocessor pastes them in textually. Each header starts with an include guard, `#pragma once` (supported everywhere) or the classic `#ifndef X_H / #define X_H / #endif`, so it isn't processed twice in one translation unit.

The **one-definition rule (ODR)**: a non-inline function or variable may be defined only once in the whole program. If you put `int helper() { ... }` in a header included by two `.cpp` files, the linker reports "multiple definition". Things that may appear in headers, because they're implicitly or explicitly `inline`, are class definitions, templates, `inline` functions, `constexpr` functions, member functions defined inside a class body, and C++17 `inline` variables. Their definitions must be identical everywhere; violating that is undefined behaviour with no diagnostic.

**Namespaces** group names and prevent clashes: `namespace geo { ... }`, used as `geo::distance`. C++17 lets you write nested ones as `namespace app::net { }`. Never write `using namespace` in a header, because it leaks into every file that includes it. In a `.cpp` file, a targeted `using std::string;` is fine.

An **unnamed namespace**, `namespace { ... }`, gives its contents internal linkage: visible only inside that `.cpp`. Use it for file-local helpers (the modern replacement for `static` functions).

C++20 **modules** (`export module geo;` / `import geo;`) and C++23's `import std;` aim to replace headers with faster, isolated compilation. Compiler and build-tool support is improving, but headers remain the norm.
takeaways: Headers declare, source files define; guard every header with `#pragma once`
Only inline things (classes, templates, `inline`/`constexpr` functions) may be defined in headers
Use an unnamed namespace for file-local helpers; never `using namespace` in a header
pitfalls: Defining a normal function in a header and getting "multiple definition" link errors once two files include it.

quiz.q: `int counter = 0;` is placed in a header included by a.cpp and b.cpp. What happens?
options: Each file gets its own counter
Compile error in the second file
It works; the compiler merges them
The linker reports a multiple-definition error
quiz.explain: It's a non-inline definition with external linkage in two translation units, violating the ODR; `inline int counter = 0;` would fix it.

quiz.q: What does wrapping a helper function in `namespace { }` in a .cpp file do?
options: Puts it in the global namespace
Makes it visible only within that translation unit
Makes it usable before its declaration
quiz.explain: Names in an unnamed namespace have internal linkage, so other files can't see or clash with them.

concepts.name: Exceptions
concepts.summary: Report errors with throw, handle them with try/catch, and rely on RAII and noexcept for exception-safe code.
concepts.why: Exceptions are the standard library's error mechanism, so you need to handle them even if your own code reports errors differently.
concepts.body:
`throw` signals an error that the current function can't handle. Control leaves the function and unwinds the stack until a matching `catch` is found; along the way every fully constructed local object is destroyed. That's why RAII matters: destructors free memory, close files and release locks during unwinding, so you don't need cleanup code at each exit.

Throw objects derived from `std::exception` (header `<stdexcept>` has `std::runtime_error`, `std::invalid_argument`, `std::out_of_range` and others), and **catch by const reference**: `catch (const std::exception& e)`. Catching by value slices derived exceptions and copies them. Handlers are tried in order, so put specific types first. `catch (...)` catches anything; inside a handler, `throw;` rethrows the current exception.

If no handler is found, `std::terminate` ends the program.

`noexcept` declares that a function won't throw; if it does, the program terminates. Destructors are `noexcept` by default. Mark move constructors and move assignment `noexcept` too, because containers like `std::vector` only move elements during reallocation when the move can't throw.

Think about **exception-safety guarantees**:

- Basic: after an exception nothing leaks and objects are still valid.
- Strong: the operation either succeeds or has no effect (commit-or-rollback, often via copy-and-swap).
- Nothrow: the operation never fails.

On mainstream compilers exceptions are "zero-cost" when nothing is thrown, but throwing is slow (microseconds). Use them for exceptional failures such as a missing config file or out of memory, not for normal control flow like "key not found". Some codebases (games, embedded) disable them, which is why the Advanced lessons cover `std::optional` and `std::expected`.
takeaways: Throw `std::exception`-derived types; catch by `const&`, most specific first
Stack unwinding runs destructors, so RAII makes code exception-safe
Mark move operations `noexcept`; use exceptions for exceptional failures only
pitfalls: Catching `std::exception` before `std::out_of_range`, so the specific handler is never reached.

quiz.q: Why should a move constructor be marked noexcept?
options: It's required for the class to be movable
std::vector only moves elements during reallocation if moving can't throw; otherwise it copies
It makes the move constructor inline
noexcept functions can't be called from catch blocks
quiz.explain: To keep the strong guarantee, vector falls back to copying unless the element's move constructor is noexcept.

quiz.q: A function throws while a std::vector, a std::unique_ptr and an open std::ofstream are local variables. What happens to them?
options: Their destructors run during stack unwinding, freeing memory and closing the file
They leak unless caught in the same function
Only the unique_ptr is cleaned up
quiz.explain: Unwinding destroys all fully constructed locals, and these RAII types release their resources in their destructors.

concepts.name: Building with CMake
concepts.summary: Describe a project with targets in CMakeLists.txt, set the C++ standard and warnings, link libraries and run tests.
concepts.why: CMake is the de-facto build system for C++; nearly every library and IDE speaks it.
concepts.body:
Compiling by hand stops scaling after a few files. **CMake** is a build-system generator: you describe your project in `CMakeLists.txt`, and CMake generates Ninja files, Makefiles or Visual Studio projects. IDEs (CLion, VS Code, Visual Studio) open CMake projects directly.

Modern CMake is all about **targets**:

- `add_executable(app main.cpp)` and `add_library(core STATIC a.cpp b.cpp)` define targets.
- `target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core)` links them, and also pulls in core's public include paths and flags.
- `target_include_directories`, `target_compile_options` and `target_compile_definitions` attach settings to one target.

The keywords matter. `PRIVATE` applies only to this target, `PUBLIC` applies to it and everything that links to it, and `INTERFACE` applies only to dependents. Avoid the old global commands like `include_directories()` and `add_compile_options()` in new code.

Set the standard with `set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)`, `CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON` and `CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF` (so you get `-std=c++20`, not `-std=gnu++20`). `CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS` writes `compile_commands.json`, which clangd and clang-tidy use.

Dependencies come in through `find_package(Foo CONFIG REQUIRED)` for installed packages (often via vcpkg or Conan), or `FetchContent` to download and build a dependency as part of your project.

Always build **out of source**: `cmake -S . -B build` configures into a separate `build` directory, `cmake --build build` compiles only what changed, and `ctest` runs tests registered with `add_test`. Choose `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug` or `Release` with single-config generators. CMake presets (`CMakePresets.json`) let a team share these settings.
concepts.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(inventory LANGUAGES CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)
set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)        # compile_commands.json for tools

add_library(core STATIC src/inventory.cpp src/storage.cpp)
target_include_directories(core PUBLIC include)   # users of core see include/
if(MSVC)
  target_compile_options(core PRIVATE /W4)
else()
  target_compile_options(core PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic)
endif()

find_package(fmt CONFIG REQUIRED)            # an installed dependency
add_executable(app src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core fmt::fmt)

enable_testing()
add_executable(core_tests tests/core_tests.cpp)
target_link_libraries(core_tests PRIVATE core)
add_test(NAME core_tests COMMAND core_tests)

# cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
# cmake --build build -j
# ctest --test-dir build
takeaways: Think in targets: `add_library`/`add_executable` + `target_*` commands
`PRIVATE` / `PUBLIC` / `INTERFACE` control what propagates to dependents
Configure out of source: `cmake -S . -B build`, then `cmake --build build`
pitfalls: Using global `include_directories()` and raw `CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS` edits instead of per-target settings.

quiz.q: Library `core` has `target_include_directories(core PUBLIC include)`. App links core with `target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core)`. Can app's sources include headers from core's include/ directory?
options: Only if app also calls include_directories
Yes, because core declared that include directory PUBLIC
quiz.explain: PUBLIC usage requirements propagate to anything that links the target; app's PRIVATE only stops it propagating further.

quiz.q: Why set CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF?
options: So the compiler uses standard -std=c++20 instead of the GNU dialect -std=gnu++20
quiz.explain: With extensions on, GCC and Clang get -std=gnu++20, which accepts non-standard extensions.

concepts.name: Move semantics and rvalue references
concepts.summary: Transfer resources instead of copying them: rvalue references, std::move, move constructors and copy elision.
concepts.why: Move semantics is why returning big objects by value is cheap in modern C++, and you need it to write efficient resource-owning types.
concepts.body:
Copying a `std::vector` duplicates all its elements. But if the source is about to die anyway, such as a temporary or a local being returned, we could just steal its heap buffer. **Move semantics** does exactly that.

Expressions have value categories. An **lvalue** has a name and an identity (`x`, `v[0]`); an **rvalue** is a temporary (`f()`, `a + b`, `Buffer(8)`). An **rvalue reference**, `T&&`, binds only to rvalues, so overloads can tell "copy from something that stays alive" from "take from something that's going away":

- `T(const T&)` is the copy constructor; `T(T&&)` is the move constructor, which takes the resource and leaves the source empty but valid.
- The same pair exists for assignment operators.

`std::move(x)` doesn't move anything. It's a cast to `T&&` that says "I'm done with `x`, you may steal from it". After a move, the object is in a **valid but unspecified** state: you may destroy it or assign a new value, but don't rely on its contents. (Standard containers do document that a moved-from vector is empty.)

Rules that matter:

- Mark move operations `noexcept`, or `std::vector` will copy instead of move when it grows.
- Return locals by plain `return x;`. The compiler elides the copy (NRVO) or moves implicitly. Writing `return std::move(x);` can block the elision.
- Since C++17, returning or initializing from a prvalue (`return Buffer(1024);`) is guaranteed to construct in place, with no copy or move at all.
- Moving a `const` object silently copies, because `const T&&` can't bind to the move constructor.

For functions that store their argument, a common idiom is to take it by value and move it in: `void set(std::string s) { name_ = std::move(s); }`.
takeaways: `std::move` is only a cast; the move constructor does the stealing
Moved-from objects are valid but unspecified: assign or destroy them only
Return locals by name; don't `return std::move(local);`
Move operations should be `noexcept`
pitfalls: Calling `std::move` on a `const` object and getting a silent copy.

quiz.q: What does `std::move(x)` do by itself?
options: Moves x's contents into a temporary
Casts x to an rvalue reference so a move overload can be chosen
Sets x to its default value
quiz.explain: std::move is just a static_cast<T&&>; nothing happens until a move constructor or assignment uses it.

quiz.q: Why is `return std::move(local);` usually worse than `return local;`?
options: It can prevent copy elision (NRVO), forcing a move
It leaves local in an invalid state
quiz.explain: Return of a named local is already elided or implicitly moved; the explicit cast disables NRVO.

concepts.name: Rule of zero, three and five
concepts.summary: Decide which special member functions a class needs, prefer letting members manage resources, and use =default and =delete.
concepts.why: Getting the special members wrong causes double frees, leaks and silent slow copies; these rules make it systematic.
concepts.body:
The compiler can generate five special members besides the default constructor: the destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor and move assignment. Which ones it generates depends on what you declare yourself.

**Rule of three/five.** If a class needs a custom destructor, it almost certainly owns a resource directly, so the generated copy operations (which copy the raw pointer) would be wrong. Define or delete all five together. Declaring any of the destructor or copy operations suppresses the implicit move operations, so a class that only adds a destructor quietly becomes copy-only.

**Rule of zero.** Better: don't own resources directly. Make every member manage itself, such as `std::string`, `std::vector`, `std::unique_ptr` or a small RAII wrapper, and declare none of the five. The generated versions then do the right thing member by member, and the class is copyable or move-only exactly when its members are. Most classes in good C++ code follow the rule of zero.

Write the full five only for a class whose job *is* to manage one resource, like a buffer or a handle wrapper. Tools that help:

- `= default` asks for the generated version explicitly (and keeps it trivial when possible).
- `= delete` forbids an operation: `T(const T&) = delete;` makes a type non-copyable.
- **Copy-and-swap**: take the assignment parameter by value and swap with it. One operator covers copy and move assignment and gives the strong exception guarantee.
- `std::exchange(o.p_, nullptr)` reads the source pointer and nulls it in one step in move constructors.

A polymorphic base declares `virtual ~Base() = default;`, which suppresses moves, so default them explicitly if the hierarchy needs to be movable.
takeaways: Rule of zero: compose RAII members and declare no special members
Rule of five: a custom destructor means you must handle copy and move too
Declaring a destructor or copy operation suppresses implicit moves
pitfalls: Adding an empty `~T() {}` "for debugging" and silently turning every move of T into a copy.

quiz.q: A class holds `std::vector<int>` and `std::unique_ptr<Foo>` and declares no special members. What can you do with it?
options: Copy it but not move it
Move it but not copy it
quiz.explain: The generated copy constructor is deleted because unique_ptr is non-copyable, while moves are generated member-wise.
