quiz.q: A class declares only a destructor `~T();`. What happens to `T b = std::move(a);`?
options: It copies, because the implicit move constructor isn't declared
quiz.explain: A user-declared destructor suppresses the implicit move operations, so the rvalue binds to the copy constructor instead.

concepts.name: Templates
concepts.summary: Write generic code with function and class templates, deduction, non-type parameters, CTAD and variadic templates.
concepts.why: Templates power the whole standard library; reading and writing them is essential for any serious C++ work.
concepts.body:
A **template** is a pattern from which the compiler generates code for each set of arguments you use. `template <typename T> T max_of(T a, T b)` works for any `T` supporting `<`; calling `max_of(3, 7)` **instantiates** `max_of<int>`. There's no runtime cost: each instantiation is ordinary, fully optimised code.

- **Function templates** usually deduce their arguments from the call. Deduction needs consistent types, so `max_of(2, 2.5)` fails (is `T` int or double?); write `max_of<double>(2, 2.5)`.
- **Class templates** like `std::vector<T>` parameterise a whole type. Since C++17, **CTAD** (class template argument deduction) deduces the arguments from the constructor: `std::vector v{1, 2, 3};` and `std::pair p{1, 2.5};`. C++20 extends CTAD to aggregates.
- **Non-type parameters** pass compile-time values: `template <typename T, std::size_t N> class Ring`. C++20 allows floating-point and simple class types here as well.
- **Variadic templates** take any number of arguments, `template <typename... Ts>`, and **fold expressions** combine them: `(xs + ... + 0)`.

Because the compiler needs the full definition to instantiate it, template code normally lives entirely in headers.

A template parameter written `T&&` in a deduced context is a **forwarding reference**, not an rvalue reference. It binds to anything, and `std::forward<T>(arg)` passes the argument on as an lvalue or rvalue, exactly as it came in. That's how `emplace_back` and `make_unique` pass constructor arguments through.

You can **specialise** a template for particular arguments, `template <> struct Hash<MyType> { ... };`, to give a custom implementation.

The traditional downside is error messages: a type that lacks an operation fails deep inside the template body. Concepts, next, fix that.
takeaways: Templates generate code per argument set at compile time — no runtime overhead
Template definitions go in headers
In a deduced `template <class T> f(T&& x)`, `T&&` is a forwarding reference; pass it on with `std::forward<T>(x)`
pitfalls: Declaring a template in a header and defining it in a .cpp file, then getting undefined-reference link errors.

quiz.q: Why does `max_of(2, 2.5)` fail for `template <typename T> T max_of(T a, T b)`?
options: Deduction gets int from one argument and double from the other, a conflict
quiz.explain: Each argument deduces T independently; int and double disagree, so deduction fails.

quiz.q: In `template <typename T> void wrap(T&& arg)`, what is `T&&`?
options: A forwarding reference that binds to lvalues and rvalues
quiz.explain: When T is deduced, T&& is a forwarding reference: T becomes U& for lvalues, so it binds to everything.

concepts.name: Concepts and constraints
concepts.summary: Constrain templates with C++20 concepts and requires clauses for clear errors and overloading by capability.
concepts.why: Concepts turn template errors from pages of noise into one line and document what a template actually needs.
concepts.body:
A **concept** is a named compile-time predicate on types. `std::integral<T>` is true for integer types; `std::totally_ordered<T>` for types with all comparisons. The header `<concepts>` provides the core set (`same_as`, `convertible_to`, `derived_from`, `invocable`, `regular`...), and `<iterator>` and `<ranges>` add many more.

You can constrain a template in several equivalent ways:

- `template <std::integral T> T half(T x);`
- `template <typename T> requires std::integral<T> T half(T x);`
- Abbreviated: `auto half(std::integral auto x);`

If a call doesn't satisfy the constraint, the error names the failed concept at the call site instead of failing somewhere inside the template body.

Define your own with a **requires-expression**, which lists the operations a type must support:

```cpp
template <typename T>
concept Shape = requires(const T& s) {
    { s.area() } -> std::convertible_to<double>;
};
```

Each requirement must compile for the concept to hold; the `-> concept` part also checks the result type.

Constraints take part in overload resolution. You can write one `half` for integers and one for floating-point types, and the right one is picked; when one constraint **subsumes** another (it includes it via `&&`), the more constrained overload wins. This replaces most uses of SFINAE and `enable_if`.

Concepts are checked structurally: a type satisfies `Shape` if it has the right members, without inheriting from anything. That's static duck typing with good errors.

Use the standard concepts when they fit, and design your own around meaningful abstractions ("a Shape", "a Sortable range") rather than single operations.
takeaways: Constrain templates with `template <Concept T>`, `requires`, or `Concept auto`
Define concepts with requires-expressions listing the needed operations
Constraints participate in overload resolution and replace most SFINAE
pitfalls: Writing a concept for a single syntactic operation ("HasPlus") instead of a meaningful abstraction.

quiz.q: What happens when you call `half("text")` with only the two constrained overloads above?
options: It compiles but fails at run time
Compile error: no overload's constraints are satisfied
quiz.explain: const char* is neither integral nor floating point, so both candidates are removed and no viable function remains.

quiz.q: A type `Circle` has `double area() const` and `std::string name() const` but no base class. Does it satisfy the Shape concept above?
options: No, it must derive from Shape
Yes, concepts check the required expressions structurally
quiz.explain: Concept satisfaction is checked by whether the requirements compile; no inheritance or registration is involved.

concepts.name: Ranges and views
concepts.summary: Use C++20 ranges: algorithms on whole containers with projections, and lazy, composable views joined with |.
concepts.why: Ranges make data pipelines shorter and safer than iterator pairs, and views avoid building temporary containers.
concepts.body:
C++20's `<ranges>` brings two big improvements.

**Range algorithms.** Everything in `std::ranges::` accepts a whole container: `std::ranges::sort(v)` instead of `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end())`. They're constrained with concepts, so misuse produces readable errors, and they accept **projections**, a function applied to each element before comparing. `std::ranges::sort(staff, {}, &Employee::age)` sorts by age with no lambda; `std::ranges::find(staff, "Mo", &Employee::name)` finds by name.

**Views.** A view is a lightweight, lazy range adaptor that doesn't own elements and computes them on demand. Compose them with `|`:

- `views::filter(pred)`, `views::transform(f)`, `views::take(n)`, `views::drop(n)`, `views::reverse`
- `views::iota(a, b)` generates numbers; `views::iota(1)` counts forever (fine when combined with `take`)
- `views::keys` / `views::values` on maps, `views::split`, `views::join`

Nothing runs until you iterate, and each element flows through the whole pipeline individually, with no intermediate vectors. C++23 adds `views::zip`, `views::enumerate`, `views::chunk`, `views::slide`, and `std::ranges::to<std::vector>()` to collect a view into a container.

Things to watch:

- Views refer to their underlying data. A view over a container must not outlive it, just like an iterator.
- Some views (such as `filter`) cache their `begin()` and must be non-const to iterate; pass views to functions by value or forwarding reference rather than `const&`.
- Range algorithms called on a temporary container return `std::ranges::dangling` instead of an iterator, so the compiler stops you from using a dangling result.
takeaways: `std::ranges::` algorithms take whole ranges and support projections
Views are lazy and non-owning; compose them with `|`
A view must not outlive the data it looks at
pitfalls: Returning a view over a local container from a function — the view dangles once the container is destroyed.

quiz.q: When does the filter lambda in `auto v = nums | std::views::filter(pred);` run?
options: When v is copied into a vector automatically
quiz.explain: Views are lazy: elements are filtered on demand as the iteration reaches them.

quiz.q: What does `std::ranges::sort(people, {}, &Person::height)` do?
options: Sorts people by height using the default less-than comparator
Sorts heights into a new vector
Doesn't compile: the comparator can't be {}
quiz.explain: {} is the default std::ranges::less, and the projection compares the height members while sorting the Person objects.

concepts.name: constexpr and compile-time code
concepts.summary: Run code at compile time with constexpr, consteval and constinit, and check assumptions with static_assert.
concepts.why: Moving work and checks to compile time catches bugs earlier and removes runtime cost, and modern C++ lets you do it with normal code.
concepts.body:
A `constexpr` function can be evaluated by the compiler when its arguments are constants, and is an ordinary function otherwise. Modern `constexpr` allows loops, local variables, `if`, `switch`, and since C++20 even virtual calls, `try` blocks, and `std::vector`/`std::string` used temporarily within the evaluation.

- `constexpr` variables must be initialized with a constant expression and are implicitly `const`. They can size arrays, be template arguments and be used in `static_assert`.
- `static_assert(cond, "msg")` fails the build if `cond` is false, documenting assumptions about sizes, layouts and constants.
- C++20 `consteval` makes an **immediate function**: every call must be evaluated at compile time. Use it when a runtime call would be a mistake, like validating format strings.
- C++20 `constinit` guarantees a global is initialized at compile time (avoiding the static initialization order problem) while staying mutable.
- `if constexpr (cond)` discards the untaken branch at compile time inside templates, so it doesn't even need to compile for that type.

A nice trick is building lookup tables with an immediately invoked lambda: `constexpr auto table = [] { ... return t; }();`. The table is computed by the compiler and stored in the binary.

A huge benefit: undefined behaviour isn't allowed in constant evaluation. Overflow, out-of-bounds access and use of uninitialized values become compile errors, so `static_assert` tests of constexpr functions double as UB checks.

`std::is_constant_evaluated()` (C++20) and C++23's `if consteval` let a function choose a different implementation at compile time, for example avoiding intrinsics the compiler can't evaluate.

Compile-time work isn't free: it costs build time, and compilers limit evaluation steps. Use it for tables, validation and configuration, not big computations.
takeaways: `constexpr` functions run at compile time when given constants, at run time otherwise
`consteval` forces compile time; `constinit` forces static initialisation
UB is a compile error in constant evaluation, so `static_assert` tests catch it
pitfalls: Assuming a `constexpr` function call is always computed at compile time — only contexts that require a constant guarantee it.

quiz.q: `constexpr int sq(int x) { return x * x; }` is called as `sq(n)` where n is read from std::cin. What happens?
options: Compile error: n is not a constant
The compiler reads n at build time
It runs at run time like a normal function
quiz.explain: constexpr allows compile-time evaluation but doesn't require it; with a runtime argument it is an ordinary call.

quiz.q: Which keyword makes every call of a function a compile-time evaluation?
quiz.explain: consteval declares an immediate function; a call that can't be evaluated at compile time is an error.

concepts.name: optional, variant and expected
concepts.summary: Model maybe-values with std::optional, one-of-several types with std::variant and std::visit, and errors as values with C++23 std::expected.
concepts.why: These vocabulary types replace sentinel values, null pointers and many exceptions with types the compiler checks.
concepts.body:
**`std::optional<T>`** (C++17) holds either a `T` or nothing. It's the clear return type for "might not have a result": `std::optional<int> parse_int(std::string_view)`. Test it with `if (opt)` or `has_value()`, read it with `*opt` (unchecked) or `opt.value()` (throws `std::bad_optional_access`), and supply a fallback with `value_or(x)`. The value is stored inline, so there's no heap allocation. C++23 adds monadic chaining: `and_then`, `transform` and `or_else`.

**`std::variant<A, B, C>`** (C++17) holds exactly one of several types, a type-safe tagged union, also stored inline. It is a closed alternative to inheritance: no virtual functions, no heap, and the set of types is fixed.

- `std::holds_alternative<B>(v)` tests the active type, `std::get<B>(v)` reads it (throws if wrong), `std::get_if<B>(&v)` returns a pointer or null.
- `std::visit(visitor, v)` calls the visitor with the active alternative. With the **overloaded** helper (a struct inheriting from several lambdas) you write one lambda per type, and forgetting a type is a compile error.

**`std::expected<T, E>`** (C++23, `<expected>`) holds either a value or an error of type `E`. It reports failure without exceptions while keeping the reason:

```cpp
std::expected<Config, std::string> load(std::string_view path);
auto cfg = load("app.toml");
if (!cfg) log(cfg.error());
```

Return `std::unexpected(err)` to signal failure. It has the same monadic operations as optional.

Which to use: exceptions for rare failures far from where they're handled; `optional` when absence needs no explanation; `expected` when callers handle errors right away and need the reason; `variant` for states and messages with a fixed set of shapes.
takeaways: `optional<T>`: a value or nothing; `value_or` gives a fallback
`variant` + `std::visit`: a closed set of types, checked exhaustively
C++23 `expected<T, E>`: a value or an error, without exceptions
pitfalls: Calling `*opt` without checking — dereferencing an empty optional is undefined behaviour.

quiz.q: A lookup may find nothing, and the caller just needs to know whether it did. Which return type fits best?
quiz.explain: optional expresses "value or nothing" with no extra error information and no allocation.

quiz.q: What does std::visit with an `overloaded` set of lambdas give you over a chain of holds_alternative checks?
options: A compile error if an alternative is not handled
quiz.explain: visit must be callable for every alternative, so a missing lambda fails to compile.

concepts.name: Threads, mutexes and atomics
concepts.summary: Run work in parallel with std::jthread, protect shared data with mutexes and scoped locks, and use atomics for simple counters.
concepts.why: Multicore hardware is the norm, and data races are undefined behaviour, so correct synchronisation is a core skill.
concepts.body:
`std::thread` starts a function on a new thread. You must `join()` it (wait) or `detach()` it before the `std::thread` object is destroyed, or the program calls `std::terminate`. C++20's **`std::jthread`** joins automatically in its destructor (RAII again) and supports cooperative cancellation: the thread function can take a `std::stop_token` and poll `stop_requested()`, and `request_stop()` asks it to finish. Prefer `jthread`.

When threads share data and at least one writes, you need synchronization. An unsynchronized concurrent read and write is a **data race**, which is undefined behaviour, not just a wrong number.

- `std::mutex` provides mutual exclusion. Never call `lock()`/`unlock()` by hand; use `std::scoped_lock lock{m};` (C++17), which unlocks at scope exit even on exceptions. `scoped_lock` can lock several mutexes at once without deadlock. Use `std::unique_lock` when you need to unlock early or wait on a condition variable.
- `std::condition_variable` lets a thread sleep until another notifies it that a condition (checked under the mutex) has become true.
- `std::atomic<T>` makes individual operations on small values (`++`, `load`, `store`, `fetch_add`, `compare_exchange`) indivisible without a lock. Good for counters and flags; for invariants spanning several variables, use a mutex.

Higher-level tools: `std::async` returns a `std::future` with the result; C++20 adds `std::latch`, `std::barrier` and `std::counting_semaphore`.

Practical advice: share as little as possible, hold locks briefly and never call unknown code while holding one, and pass data to threads by value. Capturing locals by reference in a thread lambda is only safe if the thread is joined before those locals die. Test with `-fsanitize=thread`, which detects data races at run time.
takeaways: A data race (unsynchronised write + access) is undefined behaviour
Prefer `std::jthread`; lock with `std::scoped_lock`, never manual lock/unlock
Atomics for single counters/flags, mutexes for multi-variable invariants
pitfalls: Letting a `std::thread` object be destroyed while still joinable, which calls `std::terminate`.

quiz.q: Two threads each run `++count;` 1000 times on a plain `int count = 0;`. What is guaranteed?
options: The second thread waits for the first
Nothing: it's a data race, which is undefined behaviour
quiz.explain: Unsynchronised concurrent writes are a data race; the standard gives no guarantee at all, not even a range.

quiz.q: What advantage does std::jthread have over std::thread?
options: It joins automatically in its destructor and supports stop tokens
quiz.explain: jthread is the RAII version of thread and adds cooperative cancellation via std::stop_token.

concepts.name: Undefined behaviour
concepts.summary: Know what undefined behaviour is, the common ways to trigger it, why optimisers make it dangerous, and the tools that find it.
concepts.why: UB is the source of C++'s worst bugs and security holes; experienced developers recognise the patterns on sight.
concepts.body:
The C++ standard sorts program behaviour into categories. **Implementation-defined** behaviour, like `sizeof(long)`, varies by platform but is documented. **Unspecified** behaviour, like the evaluation order of function arguments, is one of several allowed outcomes. **Undefined behaviour (UB)** means the standard places no requirements at all: the program may crash, appear to work, or do something bizarre.

The danger is the optimiser. Compilers assume UB never happens and optimise on that assumption. If `x + 1 < x` can only be true by overflowing a signed int, the compiler may fold it to `false`. If you dereference a pointer and later check it for null, the check may be deleted. UB can also appear to "travel back in time" and affect code that ran before it.

Common sources:

- Signed integer overflow, division by zero, shifting by the type's width or more.
- Out-of-bounds access (`v[i]`, raw arrays, pointer arithmetic beyond the array).
- Null, dangling or freed pointers and references, including iterators invalidated by `push_back` and `string_view`s into dead strings.
- Reading an uninitialized variable. (C++26 makes this "erroneous behaviour" with defined consequences, but it's still a bug.)
- Data races between threads.
- Breaking strict aliasing (reading a `float` through a `uint32_t*`) and other object-lifetime violations.
- Modifying a const object, or infinite loops without side effects.

Your defences: compile with `-Wall -Wextra`; test with `-fsanitize=address,undefined` (and `thread` for races); run static analysers like clang-tidy; use checked accessors (`at()`) in non-critical paths and hardened standard library modes; and prefer RAII and value types that make lifetime errors hard to write. `constexpr` evaluation also rejects UB, so compile-time tests catch it.
takeaways: UB means no guarantees; the optimiser assumes it never happens
Usual suspects: overflow, out of bounds, dangling pointers/refs, uninitialised reads, data races
Sanitizers (`-fsanitize=address,undefined,thread`) and warnings find most of it
pitfalls: Concluding code is fine because it "works on my machine" — UB can change behaviour with a new compiler, flag or input.

quiz.q: `int* p = get(); int v = *p; if (p == nullptr) return;` — what may an optimising compiler do?
options: Move the null check before the dereference
Remove the null check, since p was already dereferenced and so can't be null
Insert a runtime null check automatically
quiz.explain: Dereferencing null is UB, so the compiler may assume p is non-null and delete the later check.

quiz.q: Which of these is implementation-defined rather than undefined?
options: Reading past the end of an array
quiz.explain: The size of long varies by platform but is documented; the others are undefined behaviour.

concepts.name: Memory model and atomic ordering
concepts.summary: Understand happens-before, and choose between seq_cst, acquire/release and relaxed memory orders for atomics.
concepts.why: Lock-free code and fast synchronisation depend on memory ordering; getting it wrong produces bugs that appear only on some CPUs and some days.
concepts.body:
Compilers and CPUs reorder memory operations freely as long as a single thread can't tell. Other threads can. The C++ **memory model** defines what one thread is guaranteed to see of another's writes, through the **happens-before** relation. A program without data races behaves as if operations were interleaved in an order consistent with happens-before; a program with a data race has undefined behaviour.

Atomic operations take a `std::memory_order`:

- `seq_cst` (the default): all seq_cst operations appear in one global order that every thread agrees on. The easiest to reason about, and a bit more expensive on weakly ordered CPUs (ARM, POWER) and for stores on x86.
- `release` (on stores) and `acquire` (on loads): if an acquire load reads the value written by a release store, everything the writer did before the store **happens-before** everything the reader does after the load. This is the publish/subscribe pattern behind mutexes, queues and one-time initialization.
- `relaxed`: the operation itself is atomic, but there are no ordering guarantees for other memory. Fine for statistics counters and for compare-and-swap loops where only the atomic value matters.
- `acq_rel` for read-modify-write operations that both acquire and release. (`consume` exists but compilers treat it as `acquire`, and it's being removed.)

x86 is strongly ordered, so a missing acquire/release often only shows up on ARM, which is a good reason to rely on the model rather than on testing.

`compare_exchange_weak(expected, desired)` is the building block of lock-free algorithms. On failure it loads the current value into `expected`, so it belongs in a loop; the weak form can fail spuriously and is cheaper on LL/SC architectures. C++20 also adds `atomic::wait`/`notify_one` for efficient blocking and `std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>>`.

Start with mutexes or seq_cst; weaken orderings only with a proof and a benchmark.
takeaways: A release store read by an acquire load makes all prior writes visible
`relaxed` = atomicity only; fine for counters, wrong for publishing data
Default `seq_cst` is easiest; weaken only with proof and measurements
pitfalls: Publishing data with a relaxed flag: it may work on x86 and fail on ARM.

quiz.q: In the producer/consumer above, both orders are changed to memory_order_relaxed. What is the consequence?
options: The consumer may see ready == true but read a stale payload — a data race on payload
quiz.explain: Relaxed operations create no happens-before edge, so the payload write isn't guaranteed to be visible and the access races.

quiz.q: Why is compare_exchange_weak normally called in a loop?
options: It only works on every second call
It may fail spuriously and, on failure, updates expected with the current value to retry with
It blocks until the value changes
quiz.explain: The weak form can fail even when the values match, and the refreshed expected value lets the loop retry correctly.

concepts.name: Template metaprogramming and SFINAE
concepts.summary: Compute with types: type traits, SFINAE and enable_if, the detection idiom, if constexpr, and how concepts replace them.
concepts.why: Library code and older codebases are full of these techniques, and they explain how the standard library makes compile-time decisions.
concepts.body:
**Template metaprogramming** uses templates to compute with types and constants at compile time. The standard toolkit lives in `<type_traits>`: predicates like `std::is_integral_v<T>`, `std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T>` and `std::is_base_of_v<B, D>`; transformations like `std::remove_cvref_t<T>`, `std::decay_t<T>` and `std::conditional_t<cond, A, B>`; and `std::integral_constant` / `std::bool_constant` as the base for writing your own traits.

**SFINAE**, "substitution failure is not an error", is the rule that makes the old techniques work. While the compiler substitutes template arguments into a candidate's *signature*, an invalid type or expression just removes that candidate from overload resolution instead of causing an error. Errors inside the function *body* are still hard errors.

- `std::enable_if_t<cond, int> = 0` as a template parameter enables an overload only when `cond` holds.
- The **detection idiom** uses partial specialisation with `std::void_t<decltype(expr)>` to ask "does this expression compile?": if it does, the specialisation that inherits from `std::true_type` is chosen.
- `decltype` and `std::declval<T>()` let you form expressions on types without creating objects.

C++17 `if constexpr` removed much of the need for overload tricks: the discarded branch isn't instantiated, so it may contain code that wouldn't compile for that `T`. Fold expressions replaced most recursive variadic templates.

C++20 concepts replace the rest. `template <std::integral T>` says what `enable_if` used to say, with better errors and real subsumption rules, and a `requires` expression is the detection idiom built into the language. Write new code with concepts and `if constexpr`; learn SFINAE to read and maintain existing libraries, and for the rare cases where you still need a trait class.
takeaways: SFINAE: invalid substitution in a signature drops the candidate silently
`<type_traits>` + `decltype`/`declval` are the metaprogramming toolkit
Prefer concepts and `if constexpr` in new code
pitfalls: Expecting SFINAE to apply to errors inside a function body — only the immediate signature context is SFINAE-friendly.

quiz.q: What does SFINAE do when substituting T into a candidate's return type produces an invalid type?
options: Removes that candidate from the overload set and keeps looking
Delays the error until run time
quiz.explain: Substitution failure in the immediate context isn't an error; the candidate is just not viable.

quiz.q: Why does `if constexpr (has_size<T>::value) return x.size(); else return sizeof(T);` compile for T = int?
options: The discarded branch inside a template is not instantiated
int has a hidden size() member
if constexpr converts errors into false
sizeof makes the whole function constexpr
quiz.explain: In a template, the branch not taken by if constexpr is discarded, so x.size() is never checked for int.

concepts.name: Object lifetime and layout
concepts.summary: How objects occupy memory: storage versus lifetime, construct_at and destroy_at, alignment and padding, trivial types and bit_cast.
concepts.why: Containers, allocators, serialisation and low-level optimisation all depend on the exact rules for when an object exists and how it's laid out.
concepts.body:
In C++, **storage** and **object lifetime** are separate. Memory can exist without an object in it, and an object's lifetime begins only when it's constructed and ends when its destructor runs (or its storage is reused). Accessing an object outside its lifetime is undefined behaviour, even if the bytes are still there.

That's how `std::vector` works: it allocates raw capacity, then constructs elements in place with **placement new**, `new (ptr) T(args)`, or C++20's `std::construct_at(ptr, args...)`, and destroys them with `std::destroy_at(ptr)` without freeing the memory. If you reuse storage in tricky ways (const members, a different type), `std::launder` may be needed to obtain a valid pointer to the new object.

**Layout.** Every type has a size and an alignment (`alignof`). Members are laid out in declaration order with padding inserted so each is properly aligned, and the struct's size is padded to a multiple of its alignment. Ordering members from largest to smallest alignment often shrinks a struct, which matters for big arrays. `alignas(64)` raises alignment, for example to give a variable its own cache line.

Type properties decide what's legal:

- **Trivially copyable** types (no custom copy, move or destructor) may be copied with `memcpy`.
- **Standard-layout** types have C-compatible layout, and `offsetof` works on them.
- **Implicit-lifetime** types (aggregates of scalars, for example) are created implicitly in memory from `malloc` or `memcpy` since C++20; C++23's `std::start_lifetime_as` does it explicitly.

To reinterpret bits, use C++20's `std::bit_cast<To>(from)` (or `memcpy`). Reading a `float` through a `uint32_t*` violates **strict aliasing** and is UB. C++20's `[[no_unique_address]]` lets an empty member take no space, which is how allocators and comparators get stored for free.
takeaways: Storage and lifetime are separate: construct_at begins it, destroy_at ends it
Padding follows alignment; order members largest-first to shrink structs
Use `std::bit_cast` or `memcpy` for type punning, never pointer casts
pitfalls: Using `memcpy` on a type that isn't trivially copyable (e.g. one containing a std::string).

quiz.q: What is sizeof(S) for `struct S { char c; int i; char d; };` on a typical platform with 4-byte int alignment?
quiz.explain: c at 0, 3 bytes padding, i at 4, d at 8, then padding to a multiple of 4 gives 12.

quiz.q: Which is a well-defined way to get the bit pattern of a float as a uint32_t?
options: A union, writing f and reading the integer member
quiz.explain: bit_cast copies the object representation; the pointer cast breaks strict aliasing, static_cast converts the value, and union punning is UB in C++.

concepts.name: Linking, libraries and the ABI
concepts.summary: How the linker resolves symbols, name mangling, static versus shared libraries, ABI compatibility, extern "C" and the pimpl idiom.
concepts.why: Shipping libraries, debugging link errors and upgrading compilers safely all require understanding symbols and the ABI.
concepts.body:
Each object file has a symbol table: the functions and variables it defines and those it needs. The linker matches them up. **Linkage** decides visibility: external (shared across translation units, the default for functions and globals), internal (`static` or an unnamed namespace, private to one file) or none (locals).

Overloading and namespaces mean C++ names can't be used as raw symbols, so compilers **mangle** them: `geo::area(double)` becomes `_ZN3geo4areaEd` under the Itanium C++ ABI used on Linux and macOS (MSVC has its own scheme). `nm -C` and `c++filt` demangle. `extern "C"` turns mangling off, giving a plain C symbol; use it for C interop and for stable plugin entry points.

Libraries come in two kinds. A **static library** (`.a`, `.lib`) is an archive of object files copied into the executable at link time. With GNU ld, order matters: list libraries after the objects that use them. A **shared library** (`.so`, `.dylib`, `.dll`) is loaded at run time and shared between processes. That makes its **ABI**, the binary interface, a contract.

The ABI covers calling conventions, name mangling, object layout, vtable layout and exception handling. Changing a public class's data members, adding a virtual function, or changing an inline function or template in a header breaks the ABI: existing binaries silently use the old layout. Even standard library types change, as with libstdc++'s `std::string` switch, controlled by `_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI`. Mixing code built against different standard libraries or with incompatible flags causes link errors or worse.

To keep a stable ABI, hide data behind the **pimpl** idiom (`class Widget { struct Impl; std::unique_ptr<Impl> p_; };`), so the layout lives in the `.cpp`; or expose a C API. On ELF platforms, build with `-fvisibility=hidden` and export only the public symbols.
concepts.code:
# lib.cpp:  namespace geo { double area(double r) { return 3.14159 * r * r; } }
#           extern "C" double geo_area(double r) { return geo::area(r); }
g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -fPIC -c lib.cpp -o lib.o
nm lib.o
#   T _ZN3geo4areaEd        mangled C++ name (Itanium ABI)
#   T geo_area              extern "C": plain, unmangled
nm -C lib.o                 # demangled: geo::area(double)
echo _ZN3geo4areaEd | c++filt

# static library: archive of objects, copied into the executable
ar rcs libgeo.a lib.o
g++ main.o -L. -lgeo -o app            # libraries AFTER the objects that need them

# shared library: loaded at run time, its ABI is now a contract
g++ -shared -o libgeo.so lib.o
g++ main.o -L. -lgeo -Wl,-rpath,'$ORIGIN' -o app
ldd app | grep geo

# undefined reference to `geo::area(double)'  -> definition not linked, or wrong order
# multiple definition of `helper()'           -> non-inline function defined in a header
takeaways: C++ names are mangled into symbols; `extern "C"` gives plain C symbols
Static libraries are copied in at link time; shared libraries make the ABI a contract
Pimpl or a C API keeps a library's ABI stable across changes
pitfalls: Adding a data member or virtual function to a class exported from a shared library without rebuilding all its users.

quiz.q: A shared library adds a private data member to a public class whose definition is in its header. Existing apps aren't rebuilt. What's the risk?
options: The apps still use the old object size and layout, causing memory corruption
A compile error in the apps
The dynamic loader adapts the layout automatically
quiz.explain: Code compiled against the old header allocates and accesses objects with the old size and offsets, which is an ABI break.

quiz.q: Why is `extern "C"` used for plugin entry points like `create_plugin()`?
options: It gives an unmangled symbol name that dlsym/GetProcAddress can find reliably
It allows the function to throw exceptions across the boundary
quiz.explain: C linkage turns off name mangling, so the symbol name is predictable across compilers.

concepts.name: Allocators and polymorphic memory resources
concepts.summary: Control where containers get memory: the allocator model, std::pmr memory resources, arenas and pools.
concepts.why: Allocation is often the hidden cost in hot paths; custom memory resources can make code several times faster and more predictable.
takeaways: Containers allocate through their allocator parameter
`std::pmr` puts the strategy in a runtime memory_resource, keeping one container type
Monotonic arenas make allocation a pointer bump and free everything at once
pitfalls: Letting a memory resource be destroyed while a pmr container still uses it.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of std::pmr::vector<int> over std::vector<int, MyAlloc<int>>?
options: Vectors backed by different memory resources still have the same type
quiz.explain: The resource is chosen at run time through a pointer, so the allocator strategy isn't baked into the type.

quiz.q: Why is deallocate a no-op in monotonic_buffer_resource?
options: It hands memory back to the OS immediately
It frees everything at once when the resource is destroyed or released, which makes allocation a cheap pointer bump
Deallocation happens on a background thread
quiz.explain: A monotonic arena only grows; memory is reclaimed in bulk, trading reuse for very fast allocation.

concepts.name: Coroutines under the hood
concepts.summary: How C++20 coroutines work: the coroutine frame, promise_type, coroutine_handle, awaiters, and C++23 std::generator.
concepts.why: Coroutines power async I/O frameworks and generators; using them safely requires knowing what the compiler generates.
concepts.body:
A function becomes a **coroutine** as soon as its body uses `co_await`, `co_yield` or `co_return`. It can then suspend and later resume where it left off. C++20 coroutines are stackless: locals that live across a suspension are stored in a heap-allocated **coroutine frame**, which the compiler may elide when the coroutine's lifetime is nested in the caller.

The language supplies the mechanism; libraries supply the types. The return type (say `Generator<int>`) must name a nested **`promise_type`**, which customises behaviour:

- `get_return_object()` builds what the caller receives, usually holding a `std::coroutine_handle<promise_type>`.
- `initial_suspend()` decides whether the body starts eagerly or lazily; `final_suspend()` whether the frame stays alive after finishing (it must be `noexcept`).
- `yield_value(v)`, `return_value(v)`/`return_void()` and `unhandled_exception()` handle `co_yield`, `co_return` and exceptions.

A **`std::coroutine_handle`** is a non-owning pointer to the frame, with `resume()`, `done()`, `destroy()` and `promise()`. Someone must call `destroy()` exactly once, which is why wrapper types are move-only RAII classes.

`co_await expr` uses the **awaiter** protocol: `await_ready()` (skip suspending?), `await_suspend(handle)` (store the handle somewhere, such as an I/O completion queue, to resume later) and `await_resume()` (the result). `std::suspend_always` and `std::suspend_never` are trivial awaiters.

The biggest pitfall is lifetime. Reference parameters, and lambda captures for coroutine lambdas, are not copied into the frame, so a coroutine resumed after its caller's arguments died reads dangling memory. Take parameters by value.

C++23 adds `std::generator<T>` in `<generator>`, so you rarely write generators yourself; for async work use a library such as cppcoro, Asio or the C++26 `std::execution` model.
takeaways: Any of `co_await`/`co_yield`/`co_return` makes a coroutine with a heap frame
`promise_type` customises behaviour; `coroutine_handle` resumes and destroys
Take coroutine parameters by value; references may dangle across suspensions
pitfalls: Passing a `const std::string&` to a lazily started coroutine with a temporary argument — it dangles before the body runs.

quiz.q: With `initial_suspend()` returning std::suspend_always, when does the coroutine body start running?
options: On the first resume() of its handle
Immediately when the coroutine function is called
When the return object is destroyed
quiz.explain: Suspending initially returns control to the caller before any body code runs; the body starts at the first resume.

quiz.q: Why does the Generator wrapper call h_.destroy() in its destructor?
options: The coroutine frame is not freed automatically after final suspension; the owner must destroy it
To resume the coroutine one last time
To reset the promise's current value
quiz.explain: A coroutine that suspends at final_suspend keeps its frame alive until someone calls destroy() on its handle.

concepts.name: Performance and cache-friendly code
concepts.summary: Write fast C++: measure first, then exploit caches with contiguous data, avoid needless allocations and copies, and prevent false sharing.
concepts.why: Modern CPUs are limited by memory far more than arithmetic; data layout often decides performance more than algorithms do.
concepts.body:
Rule one: **measure**. Build with optimisations (`-O2`, plus `-march=native` and link-time optimisation `-flto` where suitable), profile with `perf`, VTune or Instruments, and microbenchmark with a library like Google Benchmark that stops the optimiser deleting your test. Intuition about performance is wrong surprisingly often.

Rule two: **memory dominates**. A main-memory access costs on the order of 100 ns, versus about 1 ns for L1 cache. The CPU fetches 64-byte cache lines and prefetches sequential access patterns. So:

- Prefer contiguous containers. Iterating a `std::vector` is typically several times faster than a `std::list` or `std::map` of the same size, because every node hop can be a cache miss. Sorted vectors and flat maps often beat trees and hash tables for small and medium sizes.
- Lay out data for how it's accessed. If a loop touches only positions, a **structure of arrays** (separate `x`, `y`, `z` vectors) keeps the cache full of useful bytes, where an **array of structures** drags whole objects in. Keep hot fields together and cold ones elsewhere.
- Avoid **false sharing**: two threads writing different variables on the same cache line ping-pong it between cores. Pad per-thread data with `alignas(std::hardware_destructive_interference_size)` (or 64).

Rule three: **don't do needless work**. `reserve()` before filling vectors; pass by `const&` or `string_view`; move instead of copying; avoid `std::function` and virtual calls in the hottest loops when templates or `std::variant` will do; keep allocation out of inner loops (use arenas, see allocators).

Branch mispredictions cost about 15 cycles; branch-free code and sorted data help, and C++20's `[[likely]]` / `[[unlikely]]` are hints. Finally, check the generated assembly (Compiler Explorer) to confirm the optimiser did what you expect.
takeaways: Measure optimised builds with a profiler before changing anything
Contiguous, sequential data wins: cache misses cost ~100x a cache hit
Avoid needless allocations and copies; pad per-thread data against false sharing
pitfalls: Micro-optimising arithmetic while the real cost is cache misses from pointer-heavy data structures.

quiz.q: Two threads each increment their own counter, but the counters are adjacent members of one struct. Why can this scale poorly?
options: False sharing: both counters share a cache line that bounces between cores
quiz.explain: Writes from different cores to the same 64-byte line force constant cache-coherency traffic even though the data is distinct.

quiz.q: A physics loop reads only particle positions, but particles are stored as a vector of large structs. What layout change usually helps most?
options: Store positions in their own contiguous arrays (structure of arrays)
quiz.explain: SoA puts only the hot data into the cache lines the loop pulls in, improving bandwidth use and enabling vectorisation.
